Try Materials.Ai David Willson 06.24.2026 Manufacturing Insights Time to read: 11 min As product design cycles accelerate, the demand for large-format industrial 3D printing has shifted from rapid prototyping to functional applications. Moving beyond the constraints of consumer-grade desktop systems, large-scale 3D printing enables engineers to produce full-scale components, enclosures, jigs, and fixtures without the lead times associated with traditional tooling. What Is Large Format 3D Printing? In an industrial context, “large” format 3D printing refers to build volumes exceeding 500 mm in any dimension. While most consumer machines focus on smaller parts, large-scale 3D printing requires advanced thermal management, high-flow extrusion, or vat-based systems capable of maintaining structural integrity across larger volumes of material. Industrial 3D printing systems often accommodate parts up to 914 x 610 x 914 mm (36 x 24 x 36 in). There are two primary categories in 3D printing : consumer (“desktop scale”) and industrial additive manufacturing. Desktop-scale systems are normally entry-level solutions found in shared workspace and R&D labs. While cost-effective, many of them are limited by thermally uninsulated environments, filament flow rate constraints, and structural instability. Industrial large-format 3D printing moves the process out of the laboratory and into the production facility. These systems handle the unique processing demands of oversized printed parts with active thermal management of the print area, advanced filament extrusion dynamics, and the ability to process reinforced, high-temperature engineering thermoplastics. When designers begin laying out large 3D-printed parts, they have to consider more than just the shape of the final product. They have to think about the thermodynamic processes that will occur during the actual build. Transitioning to industrial-grade large-format printing aligns the machine’s engineering envelope with the geometry’s physics, ensuring the finished part is fully functional. 3D Printing Techniques for Large-Scale Parts By selecting the correct process, you can achieve consistent results in large-scale additive manufacturing: Large-Format FDM (Fused Deposition Modeling) Large-Format FDM is effective for fabricating lightweight manufacturing tooling, jigs/fixtures, and even massive functional parts like robotic end-effectors and structural housings. By scaling up to wide-diameter nozzles (typically 0.6 mm to 1.2 mm or larger) and high-diameter filament inputs, industrial FDM systems can process high-performance, carbon fiber-reinforced composites to deliver heavy-duty structural components. However, scaling a filament-fed FDM system up introduces a major thermodynamic bottleneck: the volumetric extrusion limit. The maximum print speed is fundamentally governed by how quickly heat can penetrate the core of a solid polymer wire as it passes through the hotend. To maintain structural integrity across a 500 mm+ build without stalling the drive gears, industrial large-format FDM printers utilize extended melt-zone hotends, dual-element heating arrays, and forced-convection active build chambers. These active thermal environments are critical for managing the inter-laminar bond strength of the part. If the ambient chamber temperature drops too far below the material’s glass transition temperature, the previously deposited bead will cool and solidify completely before the next layer arrives. This prevents the polymer chains from cross-linking and diffusing across the layer interface, resulting in brittle parts prone to splitting under load. For large-scale high-performance thermoplastic builds, maintaining tight control over this localized thermal gradient is the only way to prevent warping and ensure true structural performance. Large SLA (Stereolithography) Large SLA printing is the best option for oversized components where premium surface finishes and feature resolutions take priority. Using precise UV laser systems to cure liquid photopolymer resins, large SLA produces aesthetic prototypes, clear fluidic housings, and master patterns for low-volume urethane casting without visible layer lines. However, scaling a vat-based photopolymerization build-up introduces hydrodynamic and mechanical challenges that don’t exist on smaller platforms. Every time a new layer is cured, the build platform lifts vertically to break the vacuum seal between the freshly cured resin and the vat’s bottom membrane. For large-surface-area parts, these peel forces scale nonlinearly. If your geometry doesn’t feature robust support anchoring and deliberate cross-sectional optimization, these separation forces can tear the part completely off its scaffolding or warp fine features. Engineers must also account for low green strength. When an SLA part is inside the liquid resin vat, it exists in a partially cured, gel-like state before its final run in a UV post-curing oven. Oversized, heavy, or long overhanging features are highly susceptible to sagging, bowing, or shifting under their own weight during construction. To mitigate this green-state deflection, large SLA parts require specialized, high-density support webbing and localized wall variations designed specifically to resist gravity and peel-line dynamics. Pellet Extrusion (BAAM) When production timelines demand large volumetric deposition rates, industrial pellet extrusion—often referred to as Big Area Additive Manufacturing (BAAM)—is the most practical option. By melting raw plastic pellets directly in a high-output, screw-driven extruder mounted on a robotic arm or large gantry, these systems bypass the volumetric flow-rate limits of traditional filaments. However, this high speed comes at the expense of surface quality. Pellet systems use wide extrusion nozzles that deposit heavy plastic beads, typically 4 to 8 mm wide. This creates a very pronounced “stair-stepping” texture along the part walls. While it is an excellent, cost-effective solution for large structural foundations, foundry patterns, and heavy marine tooling, any tight-tolerance mating faces or cosmetic surfaces will require secondary CNC post-machining to achieve a functional finish. How Does Part Size Impact the Additive Manufacturing Process? Engineers must account for the following variables when 3D printing larger parts: Thermal Warp Controlling thermal warp in large-format prints requires managing the distinct cooling behaviors of different polymer structures. Amorphous thermoplastics, such as ABS or Polycarbonate , experience a gradual, linear contraction as they cool past their glass transition temperature. Because the outer shells of a large part cool faster than the insulated core, residual internal tensile stresses accumulate, leading to severe dimensional warping or bed separation. Semi-crystalline polymers like Nylon (PA12) present an even greater challenge. They undergo a sudden, sharp volumetric drop during the crystallization phase of cooling. Without an actively managed, heated build environment to slow this crystallization down, large-format parts will warp or crack along the layer lines before the print job finishes. Internal Stress Concentration The mismatch in cooling rates between the outer surface and the interior of a bulky part can create stresses that lead to internal voids or layer delamination. Proper design should remove excess bulk, and print parameters should be precisely tuned to minimize internal stresses. Mechanical Anisotropy Because all additive manufacturing processes are inherently layer-based, parts are naturally anisotropic. In standard industrial FDM profiles, you can expect about a 20% to 45% reduction in tensile strength and inter-laminar fracture toughness along the vertical Z-axis compared to the continuous X-Y plane. This performance drop happens because the polymer chains cannot fully diffuse and entangle across the layer interfaces before the previously deposited plastic cools. When engineering large, load-bearing fixtures or enclosures, you shouldn’t rely on isotropic material datasheets without accounting for print orientation. CAD models should be oriented so that primary structural stress vectors run parallel to the build plate, utilizing the continuous strength of the extruded material strands rather than relying on the weaker layer joints. Build Time Scaling In additive manufacturing, build time doesn’t always scale linearly with part volume. It scales with the cross-sectional area of each layer and the layer count, both of which depend on the Z-height. For example, doubling a part’s Z-height doubles the layer count and proportionally increases total build time, independent of volume. Part Post-Processing Large-format parts require proportionally greater effort for support removal, surface finishing, and cleaning. The increased surface area and complex internal geometries common in large prints significantly extend post-processing time. Large-Format 3D Printing Compared to Traditional Large-Scale Tooling For large-scale components, the choice between additive manufacturing and traditional tooling comes down to trade-offs between speed, volume, and cost. Additive manufacturing (3D printing) is an agile solution that allows rapid iteration of innovative new designs, while traditional methods such as injection molding and machining remain the standard in high-volume manufacturing of mechanically strong parts. Large-Format 3D Printing vs. Molding/Machining Technical Factor Large-Format 3D Printing Large Injection Molding / Machining Upfront Tooling Cost $0 (direct from CAD) Very high (large molds/fixtures) Geometric Freedom High (internal channels & lightened lattices) Constrained by tool reach or draft angles Lead Time 1 to 5 days Weeks to months (for tooling fabrication) Mechanical Isotropy Anisotropic (depends on print orientation, material, and process) Excellent (mostly uniform grain or material density) Production Volume Ideal for 1–50 parts (prototypes/fixtures) Ideal for 500+ parts (mass production) Dimensional Tolerancing Range ±0.2 mm to ±0.5 mm (Highly dependent on process, thermal management, and material) ±0.02 mm to ±0.1 mm (Governed by rigid machine geometry and tool setups) DFM Strategies for Large-Scale 3D-Printed Parts The inherent thermal and structural challenges of oversized parts demand a deliberate design approach. The following Design for Manufacturing (DFM) strategies are essential for producing large-scale 3D-printed parts that maintain dimensional accuracy and mechanical integrity. Managing Infill, Wall Topography, and Mass Reduction Avoiding 100% infill is recommended. Using gyroid or honeycomb infill reduces part mass and thermal inertia, which significantly decreases the risk of warping while maintaining the rigidity of the print. Optimizing infill patterns and maximizing the amount of contact area between the build plate and the object being printed (for bed adhesion) helps counter the effects of thermal expansion and increase stiffness. Selecting a material like carbon fiber-filled nylon can also help reduce thermal expansion relative to many standard printing materials. Structural Ribs for Large, Flat Surfaces Large, flat surfaces are prone to bowing. Instead of increasing wall thickness uniformly, add ribs or gussets to the non-critical faces of the part (typically the interior or back side) to stiffen the geometry against thermal warping while leaving the critical face smooth and uninterrupted. Splitting Large Models: Joints and Sectioning When a design exceeds a machine’s build volume, the CAD model must be subdivided into sections. A basic dovetail or puzzle joint may be sufficient for visual models, but functional jigs and enclosures require split lines treated as engineered interfaces: Design a Bond-Line Gap : Incorporate a uniform clearance of 0.1–0.2 mm between mating surfaces to allow for part tolerances and to provide space for structural epoxy or polyurethane adhesive to seat properly. Use a Hybrid Joining Strategy : Don’t rely on adhesive alone. Combine interlocking keys or dovetails with hidden mechanical fasteners—press-fit alignment pins for shear loads, and pocket screws or heat-set threaded inserts for tensile loads. Export as Multi-Body STEP Files : Export directly from your native CAD software as a multi-body STEP file to preserve geometric alignment and coordinate registration across all joint interfaces before sending files to print. Axis Orientation Strategies for Strength If a part requires a tall Z-height, orient primary stress zones to run parallel to the build plate (X-Y plane) to leverage the higher isotropic strength of the extrusion lines. This exploits the near-isotropic strength of the fused filament direction rather than relying on the weaker interlayer bonds along the Z-axis. Choosing the right material is as critical as choosing the right process. Fictiv’s Ultimate Guide to 3D Printing Materials and Applications covers material properties, process compatibility, and application-specific recommendations in detail. Secondary Processing: Joining and Finishing Large Parts When a planned product is too big to build with one print, the components must be assembled using mechanical fasteners , solvent bonding, or adhesives . A manufacturing partner that specializes in the assembly and precision finishing required to blend jointed seams can help ensure the finished part acts as a single, cohesive unit. Streamlining Large-Part Additive Manufacturing Sourcing Manufacturing large 3D-printed parts at an industrial scale involves navigating complex design, sourcing, and processing plans. Poor decisions can result in problems ranging from build plate adhesion failures to long, unpredictable print cycles. Fictiv reduces these risks through automated DFM feedback that flags geometry, design, and process mismatch issues before your part hits the printer. With access to industrial-grade build volumes and expert multi-body assembly guidance, Fictiv is your partner in scaling from initial CAD model to shop floor production. Upload your CAD model today to start a free 3DP quote. FAQs About Large Format 3D Printing What is considered “large format” in 3D printing? In an industrial context, large format typically refers to build volumes exceeding 500 mm in any single dimension. Consumer desktop machines generally fall well below this threshold, while industrial systems can accommodate parts up to 914 x 610 x 914 mm (36 x 24 x 36 in) or larger, depending on the platform and process. Fictiv’s manufacturing network includes access to industrial-grade large-format systems capable of producing parts at this scale. Which large-format 3D printing process is best for my application? It depends on your part requirements. FDM is the most versatile choice for functional tooling, jigs, and fixtures where strength and durability matter. SLA is preferred when fine detail and smooth surface finish are critical, such as for high-fidelity prototypes. Pellet extrusion is best suited for very large structural parts where build speed and material volume take priority over surface quality. How do I prevent warping in large 3D printed parts? Warping is primarily driven by uneven thermal contraction during cooling. The most effective countermeasures include using optimized infill patterns such as gyroid or honeycomb to reduce thermal mass, maximizing the bed-adhesion contact area, selecting low-shrinkage materials like carbon fiber-filled nylon, and incorporating structural ribs into large flat surfaces to resist bowing. What should I do if my part is too large for the printer’s build volume? The part will need to be sectioned in CAD and printed as multiple pieces. Design keyed joints or dovetail features at the split interfaces to ensure self-alignment and maximize bonding surface area. Export the assembly as a multi-body STP file for geometry registration, then export each section as a separate STL for printing. Sections can then be joined using mechanical fasteners, adhesives, or solvent bonding. Fictiv’s manufacturing partners specialize in precision finishing and assembly of multi-body large-format parts. How does large-format 3D printing compare to traditional machining or injection molding for large parts? For low volumes and iterative design, large-format 3D printing offers significant advantages: no upfront tooling cost, lead times of one to five days, and geometric freedom that traditional processes can’t match. However, for high-volume production of 500 or more parts, injection molding and machining remain superior due to better mechanical isotropy, tighter tolerances, and lower per-part cost at scale. Fictiv supports both additive and traditional manufacturing, making it straightforward to transition from prototype to production without switching suppliers.

CAD models should be oriented so that primary structural stress vectors run parallel to the build plate, utilizing the continuous strength of the extruded material strands rather than relying on the weaker layer joints. Build Time Scaling In additive manufacturing, build time doesn’t always scale linearly with part volume. It scales with the cross-sectional area of each layer and the layer count, both of which depend on the Z-height. For example, doubling a part’s Z-height doubles the layer count and proportionally increases total build time, independent of volume. Part Post-Processing Large-format parts require proportionally greater effort for support removal, surface finishing, and cleaning. The increased surface area and complex internal geometries common in large prints significantly extend post-processing time. Large-Format 3D Printing Compared to Traditional Large-Scale Tooling For large-scale components, the choice between additive manufacturing and traditional tooling comes down to trade-offs between speed, volume, and cost. Additive manufacturing (3D printing) is an agile solution that allows rapid iteration of innovative new designs, while traditional methods such as injection molding and machining remain the standard in high-volume manufacturing of mechanically strong parts. Large-Format 3D Printing vs. Molding/Machining Technical Factor Large-Format 3D Printing Large Injection Molding / Machining Upfront Tooling Cost $0 (direct from CAD) Very high (large molds/fixtures) Geometric Freedom High (internal channels & lightened lattices) Constrained by tool reach or draft angles Lead Time 1 to 5 days Weeks to months (for tooling fabrication) Mechanical Isotropy Anisotropic (depends on print orientation, material, and process) Excellent (mostly uniform grain or material density) Production Volume Ideal for 1–50 parts (prototypes/fixtures) Ideal for 500+ parts (mass production) Dimensional Tolerancing Range ±0.2 mm to ±0.5 mm (Highly dependent on process, thermal management, and material) ±0.02 mm to ±0.1 mm (Governed by rigid machine geometry and tool setups) DFM Strategies for Large-Scale 3D-Printed Parts The inherent thermal and structural challenges of oversized parts demand a deliberate design approach. The following Design for Manufacturing (DFM) strategies are essential for producing large-scale 3D-printed parts that maintain dimensional accuracy and mechanical integrity. Managing Infill, Wall Topography, and Mass Reduction Avoiding 100% infill is recommended. Using gyroid or honeycomb infill reduces part mass and thermal inertia, which significantly decreases the risk of warping while maintaining the rigidity of the print. Optimizing infill patterns and maximizing the amount of contact area between the build plate and the object being printed (for bed adhesion) helps counter the effects of thermal expansion and increase stiffness. Selecting a material like carbon fiber-filled nylon can also help reduce thermal expansion relative to many standard printing materials. Structural Ribs for Large, Flat Surfaces Large, flat surfaces are prone to bowing. Instead of increasing wall thickness uniformly, add ribs or gussets to the non-critical faces of the part (typically the interior or back side) to stiffen the geometry against thermal warping while leaving the critical face smooth and uninterrupted. Splitting Large Models: Joints and Sectioning When a design exceeds a machine’s build volume, the CAD model must be subdivided into sections. A basic dovetail or puzzle joint may be sufficient for visual models, but functional jigs and enclosures require split lines treated as engineered interfaces: Design a Bond-Line Gap : Incorporate a uniform clearance of 0.1–0.2 mm between mating surfaces to allow for part tolerances and to provide space for structural epoxy or polyurethane adhesive to seat properly. Use a Hybrid Joining Strategy : Don’t rely on adhesive alone. Combine interlocking keys or dovetails with hidden mechanical fasteners—press-fit alignment pins for shear loads, and pocket screws or heat-set threaded inserts for tensile loads. Export as Multi-Body STEP Files : Export directly from your native CAD software as a multi-body STEP file to preserve geometric alignment and coordinate registration across all joint interfaces before sending files to print. Axis Orientation Strategies for Strength If a part requires a tall Z-height, orient primary stress zones to run parallel to the build plate (X-Y plane) to leverage the higher isotropic strength of the extrusion lines. This exploits the near-isotropic strength of the fused filament direction rather than relying on the weaker interlayer bonds along the Z-axis. Choosing the right material is as critical as choosing the right process. Fictiv’s Ultimate Guide to 3D Printing Materials and Applications covers material properties, process compatibility, and application-specific recommendations in detail. Secondary Processing: Joining and Finishing Large Parts When a planned product is too big to build with one print, the components must be assembled using mechanical fasteners , solvent bonding, or adhesives . A manufacturing partner that specializes in the assembly and precision finishing required to blend jointed seams can help ensure the finished part acts as a single, cohesive unit. Streamlining Large-Part Additive Manufacturing Sourcing Manufacturing large 3D-printed parts at an industrial scale involves navigating complex design, sourcing, and processing plans. Poor decisions can result in problems ranging from build plate adhesion failures to long, unpredictable print cycles. Fictiv reduces these risks through automated DFM feedback that flags geometry, design, and process mismatch issues before your part hits the printer. With access to industrial-grade build volumes and expert multi-body assembly guidance, Fictiv is your partner in scaling from initial CAD model to shop floor production. Upload your CAD model today to start a free 3DP quote. FAQs About Large Format 3D Printing What is considered “large format” in 3D printing? In an industrial context, large format typically refers to build volumes exceeding 500 mm in any single dimension. Consumer desktop machines generally fall well below this threshold, while industrial systems can accommodate parts up to 914 x 610 x 914 mm (36 x 24 x 36 in) or larger, depending on the platform and process. Fictiv’s manufacturing network includes access to industrial-grade large-format systems capable of producing parts at this scale. Which large-format 3D printing process is best for my application? It depends on your part requirements. FDM is the most versatile choice for functional tooling, jigs, and fixtures where strength and durability matter. SLA is preferred when fine detail and smooth surface finish are critical, such as for high-fidelity prototypes. Pellet extrusion is best suited for very large structural parts where build speed and material volume take priority over surface quality. How do I prevent warping in large 3D printed parts? Warping is primarily driven by uneven thermal contraction during cooling. The most effective countermeasures include using optimized infill patterns such as gyroid or honeycomb to reduce thermal mass, maximizing the bed-adhesion contact area, selecting low-shrinkage materials like carbon fiber-filled nylon, and incorporating structural ribs into large flat surfaces to resist bowing. What should I do if my part is too large for the printer’s build volume? The part will need to be sectioned in CAD and printed as multiple pieces. Design keyed joints or dovetail features at the split interfaces to ensure self-alignment and maximize bonding surface area. Export the assembly as a multi-body STP file for geometry registration, then export each section as a separate STL for printing. Sections can then be joined using mechanical fasteners, adhesives, or solvent bonding. Fictiv’s manufacturing partners specialize in precision finishing and assembly of multi-body large-format parts. How does large-format 3D printing compare to traditional machining or injection molding for large parts? For low volumes and iterative design, large-format 3D printing offers significant advantages: no upfront tooling cost, lead times of one to five days, and geometric freedom that traditional processes can’t match. However, for high-volume production of 500 or more parts, injection molding and machining remain superior due to better mechanical isotropy, tighter tolerances, and lower per-part cost at scale. Fictiv supports both additive and traditional manufacturing, making it straightforward to transition from prototype to production without switching suppliers.

Manufacturing Services Blog Blog Home Blog Knowledge Hub Sheet Metal Fabrication Bending and Forming Technology in Sheet Metal Processing Published Jan 10, 2025, updated Dec 23, 2025 5 min Bending and molding techniques in plate processing are key processes for manufacturing complex shapes and structures. This article will delve into the fundamentals, different types, material suitability, technical advantages, and practical application cases of these technologies. Learn how bending and forming technologies can enhance the precision and efficiency of sheet processing and meet the high precision requirements of modern manufacturing. What is Bending and Molding Technology Bending and forming involves applying an external force to a sheet of metal to cause it to deform along a predetermined curve, thereby creating a defined geometric form. This process is carried out with the help of a bending machine, which places the sheet to be processed in the gap between the punch and the mold, and the pressure exerted by the bending machine induces the sheet to bend until it reaches the pre-determined bending angle. It is important to note that the precision and accuracy of the bending process is significantly affected by the type of material used, the thickness of the sheet, and the design of the punch and die. Types of bending and forming technology Bending machines The press brake is the most commonly used bending machine for a wide range of materials and plate thicknesses. It applies pressure by means of a hydraulic or electric system to form the desired shape of the sheet in the die. The bending machine can realize a wide range of bending shapes, such as V and U shapes, and is suitable for manufacturing complex structures with multiple bends. Automated Bending Center Automated Bending Centers are advanced metalworking machines designed for efficient production. These machines are often equipped with advanced control systems that automatically adjust bending parameters to improve productivity and consistency. Automated bending centers are particularly well suited for high volume production, reducing manual intervention and increasing productivity. Manual Bending Machines Manual bending machines are simple but effective tools used to create precise bends along a straight line. They are typically used in small shops and for repair work, and are suitable for working with thin sheet metal. Manual bending machines are easy to operate and less expensive, but have relatively low productivity and accuracy. Material suitability Bending and forming techniques are applicable to a wide range of metal materials, including steel, aluminum and stainless steel. The physical properties of these materials, such as yield strength and modulus of elasticity, influence the deformation behavior during bending. Selecting the right material and bending process ensures dimensional accuracy and structural integrity of the final product. Technical Advantages High Accuracy and Consistency Bending and molding technology enables high-precision bending and ensures consistency from part to part. This is especially important for applications that require tight tolerances, such as aerospace and automotive manufacturing. High-precision bending reduces the need for subsequent machining and increases productivity. Versatility Bend molding technology can handle a wide range of shapes and complex designs, and is suitable for manufacturing complex structures with multiple bends and features. This versatility allows manufacturers to produce unique and customized products that meet the needs of diverse customers. Reduced Costs By optimizing the design and process, bending and forming technology can reduce material waste and production costs. Precise bending reduces the need for subsequent machining, shortens production cycles and improves overall productivity. Practical Application Examples Automotive industry In the automotive industry, Bend Molding technology is used to manufacture body panels, engine components and interior trim. High-precision bending ensures dimensional accuracy and assembly compatibility of parts, improving the quality and performance of the entire vehicle. Aerospace Industry The aerospace industry requires a high degree of material precision and quality. Bending and molding technology is used to manufacture aircraft engine parts, wing structures and satellite components. High precision bending and molding technology ensures the performance and reliability of these critical components. Electronics Industry The electronics industry requires high-precision metal processing to manufacture circuit boards, housings and heat sinks. Bending and forming technology enables micron-level precision for cutting thin metals and non-metallic materials such as copper, aluminum and plastics. High-precision bending and forming technology ensures the quality and performance of electronic products. Whether you are in the automotive, aerospace or electronics industries, JLCCNC can provide you with high-quality, customized bending and molding solutions to ensure that your projects excel in a variety of applications. Conclusion Bending and forming technologies are used in a wide range of sheet metal processing applications, and their high precision, versatility, and cost-effectiveness make them important tools in modern manufacturing. By understanding the fundamentals, different types, material suitability, and practical applications of these technologies, manufacturers can better utilize this technology to improve productivity and product quality. Manufacturing Services Blog Blog Home Blog Knowledge Hub CNC Machines & Equipment Best CNC Machines for Metal: A Guide for Choosing Between Mills, Routers, and Press Brakes Published Jun 18, 2025, updated Dec 23, 2025 6 min If you're machining metal, you already know the difference between real guidance and sales fluff. Most blogs titled "Best CNC Machines for Metal" throw around specs and brand names without explaining how those factors actually affect your tolerances, cycle times, or tooling life. This guide is different. Written for engineers, machinists, and procurement teams, this breakdown skips the surface-level intro and dives straight into what matters: ● machine rigidity, ● chip load management, ● thermal response, ● torque curves, ● cost vs throughput, ● and machine-material compatibility. Let’s get into the serious stuff. What Real Metal Fabrication Demands from a CNC Machine 1. Rigidity and Frame Design CNC mills and routers might look similar at a glance, but the structural mechanics make all the difference when you're cutting steel instead of MDF. In metal work, deflection is your enemy. A cast-iron frame with linear rails and box ways maintains part tolerance under load, whereas lightweight aluminum gantries will vibrate and drift. Real-world example: If you're slotting 304 stainless with a 10mm carbide end mill at 0.1mm per tooth, even a 0.05mm deflection causes dimensional error and increases tool wear significantly. 2. Spindle Power & Torque Forget max RPM, what you care about is torque at the cutting speed. Milling steel at 60-100 SFM requires consistent torque at low RPM. Belt-driven spindles may spin faster, but lack the torque curve needed to push through alloys. Compare this: ● Hobby router spindle: 1.5 kW, 18,000 RPM, low torque below 6,000 ● VMC spindle: 7.5 kW, 8,000 RPM, 70 Nm+ torque peak at 1,800 RPM 3. Chip Evacuation & Cooling In soft material, you can get away with brushing chips aside. In steel, recutting hot chips means work hardening and broken tools. Machines built for metal will include through-spindle coolant (TSC), programmable coolant nozzles, and enclosed flood systems. CNC Mills: When Precision and Tough Materials Are Non-Negotiable CNC milling machines are the backbone of precision metal work. Verify Now Blog > Clock Circuit Design Guidelines for PCB Layout Clock Circuit Design Guidelines for PCB Layout by: Mila Nov 06,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout clock circuit crystal oscillator pcb Layout pcb clock signal routing Clock circuits play an essential role in electronic systems by providing timing signals that synchronize the operation of different components. However, improper clock circuit design can lead to signal interference, timing errors, and system instability. This article explores the PCB design guidelines for crystal circuits, active oscillators, and clock distributors, covering key considerations for component placement, signal routing, and noise reduction. 1. Crystal A clock is an essential part of any electronic system. It acts like the heartbeat of the system, providing synchronization signals to different components. If the clock signal becomes unstable or fails, the entire system may malfunction or stop working. Therefore, proper clock circuit design is essential in PCB design. Common clock sources and distribution components used in PCBs include crystals, oscillators, and clock distributors. Some ICs may generate their own clock signals internally. However, the clock signal ultimately originates from a crystal, an oscillator, or another clock source before being distributed to other components. When designing a crystal circuit, consider the following guidelines: Place the crystal as close as possible to the IC's oscillator pins to minimize trace length and reduce external interference. For designs with high electromagnetic compatibility requirements, consider using a crystal with a metal shield package. Ensure that the shield is properly grounded according to the component datasheet. Avoid routing other signal traces beneath the crystal and its load capacitors, especially high-speed digital signals. A continuous GND reference plane can be provided beneath the crystal circuit according to the IC manufacturer's layout recommendations. Keep high-speed digital signal traces away from the crystal to reduce crosstalk. Keep the ground connections of the load capacitors as short as possible to minimize parasitic inductance and provide a low-impedance return path. A GND guard area can be added around the crystal according to the recommended layout. If necessary, use GND vias to connect the ground copper on different layers. Place the crystal and its two load capacitors close to the IC's oscillator pins. Follow the component manufacturer's reference design for the exact placement arrangement. Common crystal packages used in PCB design include 2-pin through-hole packages, 2-pin SMD packages, and 4-pin SMD packages. （Common crystal package types） Although crystals are available in different package sizes and specifications, their basic operating principles and peripheral circuit designs are similar. Therefore, many PCB placement and routing guidelines are applicable across different crystal designs. A basic crystal circuit is shown below: （Basic crystal circuit schematic） The two capacitors shown in the schematic are load capacitors. They connect the two crystal terminals to ground and provide the required load capacitance for stable oscillation. Their values should be determined based on the crystal datasheet, the IC's internal oscillator characteristics, and the parasitic capacitance of the PCB. 2. Crystal Circuit Placement and Routing When placing a crystal circuit, position the two load capacitors as close as possible to the crystal and the IC's oscillator pins. This helps minimize trace length and reduce the impact of parasitic parameters. The placement is shown below: （Crystal circuit placement） When routing the crystal circuit, keep the two connections between the crystal and the IC as short as possible and preferably close to each other to reduce parasitic capacitance and external interference. Note that these two traces are not true differential signal lines, so differential routing rules should not be applied directly. Avoid unnecessary vias and follow the IC manufacturer's layout recommendations to determine whether GND guard traces are needed. The routing layout is shown below: （Crystal circuit routing） 3. Crystal Circuit Design Variations The circuit described above is the most basic and commonly used crystal circuit design. In practical PCB designs, additional components such as series resistors and test points may be included to meet debugging or signal integrity requirements. However, the basic design principles remain the same. Based on the guidelines above, consider the following points when placing components: （Crystal circuit layout with a series resistor and test point） Place the crystal, associated capacitors, and series resistor on the same PCB layer whenever possible to reduce vias and shorten connection paths. If test points are required, avoid long stubs. Additional trace branches may introduce parasitic capacitance and affect oscillator stability. Avoid placing high-power components near the crystal, such as power ICs, MOSFETs, and inductors, as heat generated by these components may affect crystal frequency stability. Routing guidelines: Place and route the crystal on the same layer as the IC whenever possible to minimize vias. If layer changes are necessary, ensure a continuous return path and add nearby GND vias when needed. Keep crystal traces as short as possible. Trace width should be determined based on the IC manufacturer's recommendations and PCB fabrication capabilities rather than increased unnecessarily. GND guard traces can be added around the crystal circuit when appropriate. Connect them to the reference ground plane using GND vias. Keep the crystal circuit area relatively isolated. Avoid routing other high-speed signals through this area to reduce crosstalk and external noise interference. 4. Oscillator Circuit Design Unlike passive crystals, active oscillators integrate an internal oscillation circuit and can directly output clock signals. An active oscillator circuit typically consists of an oscillator device, a power supply decoupling circuit, and an optional source-series resistor selected according to the output interface and load requirements. A typical oscillator circuit is shown below: （Active oscillator circuit schematic） The PCB placement and routing layout is shown below: （Active oscillator PCB layout and routing） Placement and routing guidelines: Place power decoupling capacitors as close as possible to the oscillator's power supply pins. Prioritize a short power and ground loop for the high-frequency decoupling capacitor. If multiple decoupling capacitors are used, select their capacitance values and placement based on the component datasheet and power integrity requirements. There is no need to mechanically follow a fixed large-to-small capacitor arrangement. Determine whether a source-series resistor is needed based on the oscillator's output type, drive capability, trace length, and load conditions. If required, place it as close as possible to the oscillator output pin. Determine the clock signal impedance based on the oscillator output interface, receiver requirements, and PCB stackup. For clock signals that require transmission line control, implement appropriate impedance design. For long clock traces, consider routing them on an inner layer while maintaining a continuous reference plane. If layer transitions are necessary, add nearby GND return vias when appropriate. Maintain adequate spacing between clock traces and other signal traces to reduce crosstalk. The required spacing depends on signal edge rate, trace length, and layer-to-layer coupling. For longer clock traces, GND guard traces may be used when appropriate. Ensure that the guard traces are properly grounded and do not compromise signal integrity. 5. Clock Distributor Design A clock distributor is primarily used to distribute a clock signal from a clock source to multiple ICs or functional modules. Different clock distributors vary in terms of output count, frequency range, output interface, and drive capability. During PCB design, carefully plan the placement of the clock distributor relative to the receiving ICs to minimize clock signal routing distances. For designs that require clock skew control, also consider the routing lengths and loads of different output channels. The clock distributor is often placed at a relatively central position among the receiving devices. A typical clock distributor circuit is shown below: （Clock distributor circuit schematic） The PCB layout is shown below: （Clock distributor PCB layout） Placement and routing guidelines: Place the clock generation circuit as close as possible to the clock distributor. Common clock sources include crystals, active oscillators, and other clock generation circuits. Position the clock distributor appropriately in relation to the receiving ICs to minimize clock signal routing distances. For designs requiring clock skew control, keep the routing lengths and loads of related clock output paths as consistent as possible. Avoid placing high-power components near the clock distributor, such as power ICs, MOSFETs, and inductors, as temperature variations may affect clock performance. For long clock signal traces, consider routing them on inner layers while maintaining a continuous reference plane. If layer transitions are necessary, add GND return vias close to the signal vias to provide a continuous return path. Control trace impedance and signal spacing according to the clock frequency, edge rate, and interface requirements to reduce crosstalk and signal reflections. A well-designed clock circuit is essential for maintaining stable and reliable operation in electronic systems. Whether using a crystal, an active oscillator, or a clock distributor, careful component placement, short signal paths, proper grounding, and appropriate impedance control all contribute to better clock signal integrity. By following these PCB clock circuit design guidelines, engineers can reduce noise interference, minimize signal distortion, and improve overall system stability. Verify Now Blog > Differential Pair Routing: 3 Common Design Mistakes to Avoid Differential Pair Routing: 3 Common Design Mistakes to Avoid by: Mila Nov 04,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout Differential Pair Differential Pair Routing High-Speed PCB Design Differential Pair Routing In high-speed PCB design , differential pairs are increasingly used, especially in high-speed interfaces such as USB, HDMI, and PCIe. These interfaces commonly use differential signaling for reliable data transmission. Why is differential signaling so widely used? Compared with conventional single-ended routing, differential pairs offer better noise immunity, help suppress common-mode noise and electromagnetic interference (EMI), and improve signal integrity and timing performance. Differential Pair Routing Requirements In PCB design, a differential pair consists of two closely coupled signal traces. To ensure signal transmission quality, these traces generally need to have matched lengths, equal widths, consistent spacing, and symmetrical routing. Differential impedance must also be controlled according to the design requirements. （Differential Pair Routing Requirements） 1. Equal Length Equal length means keeping the two traces in a differential pair as close in length as possible. The purpose is to control the propagation delay difference (skew) between the two signals, maintain proper timing alignment, and reduce signal imbalance and the resulting common-mode noise. 2. Equal Width and Spacing Equal width means maintaining the same trace width for both signals. Equal spacing means keeping the distance between the two traces as consistent as possible, allowing them to run symmetrically and in parallel. This helps maintain a stable coupling relationship between the two traces, minimizes differential impedance variations, and improves signal transmission quality. 3. Controlled Differential Impedance When designing a PCB with differential pairs, one of the first steps is to determine the target differential impedance required by the interface and plan the routing accordingly. It is also important to minimize impedance variations along the routing path. Differential impedance is affected by several factors, including trace width, spacing between the two traces, copper thickness, PCB material, and stackup structure. These factors should all be considered during the design process to maintain consistent differential impedance. 4. Maintain a Continuous Reference Plane Although differential signals offer strong noise immunity, they still require an appropriate reference plane. The reference plane beneath the differential pair should remain continuous whenever possible. Avoid routing differential pairs across split ground planes or slots in the reference plane, as these discontinuities can alter return paths and cause impedance variations. Common Misconceptions About Differential Pair Routing Misconception 1: Differential Signals Do Not Need a Ground Plane as a Return Path, or the Two Traces Can Serve as Each Other's Return Paths. Differential signals offer strong immunity to common-mode noise, but this does not mean they do not need a reference plane. In fact, the return-current path depends on the coupling between the two differential traces and their coupling to the reference plane. Differential-mode return current is primarily associated with the electromagnetic coupling between the two traces, while the reference plane still affects the return path and impedance characteristics, especially for common-mode currents. When the reference plane contains splits or slots, the return-current path may change, causing impedance discontinuities, signal degradation, and increased EMI. Therefore, differential pairs should be routed over a continuous reference plane whenever possible, avoiding split ground regions. In addition, removing the reference plane beneath differential traces to suppress common-mode noise is not recommended. This can make impedance control more difficult and disrupt the return path for common-mode currents, potentially increasing electromagnetic radiation. （Differential Signal Reference Plane） Misconception 2: Maintaining Consistent Spacing Is More Important Than Matching Trace Lengths. In practical PCB routing, it is not always possible to satisfy every differential pair design requirement simultaneously. Component pin placement, via locations, and available routing space may require designers to introduce serpentine routing to match trace lengths. However, this can cause some sections of the differential pair to lose their parallel alignment or consistent spacing. In such cases, design priorities should be determined according to the interface specifications and application requirements. For high-speed differential interfaces with strict intra-pair skew limits, length matching is particularly important. However, trace spacing also affects coupling and differential impedance, so it should not be overlooked. During routing, priority should be given to meeting interface timing and impedance requirements. Symmetry, consistent spacing, and routing continuity should then be maintained as much as possible, rather than focusing on just one routing parameter. （Differential Line Length Matching） Misconception 3: Differential Traces Must Always Be Routed Close Together. Routing differential traces close together strengthens the coupling between them, improving noise immunity and helping reduce electromagnetic radiation through partial magnetic field cancellation. However, closer spacing is not always better. The spacing should be determined by the target differential impedance, PCB stackup, and application requirements. Excessively small spacing may make impedance control and manufacturing more challenging. To reduce crosstalk, maintain sufficient spacing between differential pairs and other signal traces. The 4W rule (spacing of at least four times the trace width) can serve as an initial guideline, but actual spacing should be determined by the design requirements. Ground guard traces connected to the reference plane through stitching vias can also provide additional isolation. For high-frequency applications, coplanar waveguide (CPW) structures are another option for controlling differential impedance. （Differential Line Spacing） Conclusion Differential pair routing is an important part of high-speed PCB design . In addition to trace length, width, and spacing, designers must also consider differential impedance, reference-plane continuity, and interference from surrounding signals. Only by considering all these factors together can designers ensure reliable differential signal transmission and improve overall PCB performance and reliability. NTC, PTC, and PCB Layout by: Mila Nov 18,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout thermistor circuit NTC thermistor PTC thermistor NTC vs PTC thermistor thermistor pcb Temperature monitoring is essential for protecting electronic components, maintaining system stability, and ensuring reliable operation. Whether preventing a battery from overheating or keeping an industrial motor within its operating temperature range, accurate temperature sensing plays an important role. Among various temperature sensors, thermistors are widely used because of their simple structure, low cost, and fast response. This article explains how thermistors work, explores common measurement circuits, discusses key performance parameters, and compares NTC and PTC thermistors to help guide component selection and PCB design . 1. What Is a Thermistor? Understanding How It Works Working Principle: A thermistor is a resistor whose resistance changes significantly with temperature. The name comes from the combination of "thermal" and "resistor." Its key characteristic is that its resistance varies in response to changes in its own temperature. This property allows a thermistor to convert temperature, a physical quantity, into a change in electrical resistance, which can then be converted into a measurable voltage signal through an external circuit. Figure 1. Different types of thermistors Two Main Types: Based on how their resistance changes with temperature, thermistors are generally divided into two categories: NTC (Negative Temperature Coefficient) Thermistors: Their resistance decreases as temperature increases. NTC thermistors are among the most widely used temperature-sensing components due to their low cost and high sensitivity. Common applications include battery temperature monitoring, power management, and household appliance temperature control. PTC (Positive Temperature Coefficient) Thermistors: Their resistance increases as temperature rises. Depending on their materials and resistance characteristics, PTC thermistors can be further divided into two types: Nonlinear (Switching-Type) PTC Thermistors: Their resistance increases sharply near a specific temperature, known as the Curie temperature. They are commonly used for overcurrent protection, overtemperature protection, and resettable fuses. Linear PTC Thermistors: Typically made from silicon, these devices have a relatively stable positive temperature coefficient. Their resistance increases approximately linearly with temperature, making them suitable for temperature measurement applications. Simply put, an NTC thermistor behaves like a component that offers less resistance as it gets hotter. A linear PTC thermistor works in the opposite way: its resistance increases with temperature, generally in a more uniform and predictable manner. 2. How to Read a Thermistor: Two Common Measurement Circuits A thermistor does not generate an electrical signal on its own. It requires an external excitation source to convert its resistance changes into a measurable voltage signal. The following are two commonly used measurement circuits. Voltage Divider Circuit (Constant-Voltage Excitation) Figure 2. Thermistor in a voltage divider configuration This is one of the simplest and most cost-effective thermistor measurement methods. A thermistor is connected in series with a fixed reference resistor and supplied by a stable voltage source, such as VCC. By measuring the voltage across one of the resistors, the temperature information can be obtained. Working Principle: When the temperature changes, the thermistor's resistance changes accordingly. According to the voltage divider principle, the output voltage, V_TEMP, also changes. By measuring this voltage, the thermistor resistance can be calculated, and the corresponding temperature can then be determined. Advantages: The circuit is simple, requires few components, and has a low implementation cost, making it suitable for many conventional temperature-sensing applications. Considerations: Variations in the supply voltage VCC can affect V_TEMP and introduce measurement errors. To reduce this effect, a ratiometric measurement method can be used. For example, the same voltage source can serve as both the excitation voltage for the divider and the ADC reference voltage. This helps cancel out the effects of supply voltage fluctuations. Constant-Current Excitation Circuit Figure 3. Thermistor measurement using constant-current excitation Another approach is to use a precision constant-current source (I BIAS ) to supply a stable current to the thermistor. Working Principle: According to Ohm's law, V = I × R. Since the current flowing through the thermistor remains constant, the voltage across it, V_TEMP, is proportional to its resistance: V TEMP = I BIAS × R THERMISTOR When the temperature changes and the thermistor resistance varies, the output voltage changes accordingly. Advantages: Within the operating range of the current source, the output voltage is linearly proportional to the thermistor resistance. This makes resistance measurement and signal processing more straightforward, especially in applications requiring relatively high measurement accuracy. Considerations: The accuracy, temperature drift, and output voltage range of the current source all affect measurement results. In addition, excessive excitation current can cause thermistor self-heating. Therefore, the bias current must be selected carefully. The Next Step: Signal Processing The resulting analog voltage signal, V TEMP , is typically sent to an analog-to-digital converter (ADC) input on a microcontroller (MCU) for digital processing. Alternatively, it can be sent to a voltage comparator and compared with a preset threshold voltage to implement a basic overtemperature alarm. Figure 4. Overtemperature threshold detection using a thermistor and comparator 3. Key Parameters for Improving Thermistor Performance and Accuracy When selecting a thermistor, its nominal resistance is not the only parameter to consider. The following characteristics also play an important role in determining temperature measurement accuracy, stability, and overall circuit complexity. Resistance Tolerance Resistance tolerance refers to the allowable deviation between a thermistor's actual resistance and its nominal resistance at a specified temperature, typically 25°C. For example, a tolerance of ±1% means the actual resistance can vary within 1% of the specified nominal value at that temperature. NTC Thermistors: The resistance tolerance of an NTC thermistor depends not only on its nominal resistance at 25°C but also on the tolerance of its B-value and other material characteristics. Therefore, even if an NTC thermistor has a resistance tolerance of ±1% at 25°C, its actual measurement error may increase significantly at other temperatures. Linear PTC Thermistors: Some silicon-based linear PTC thermistors maintain relatively stable resistance-temperature characteristics over a wide operating temperature range, helping achieve consistent measurements. However, their actual tolerance still depends on the specific device and its datasheet specifications. Temperature Sensitivity and Measurement Resolution Sensitivity describes how much a thermistor's resistance changes in response to a change in temperature. It reflects the sensor's ability to respond to temperature variations. Measurement resolution, on the other hand, refers to the smallest temperature change that the entire measurement system can detect. NTC Thermistors: The resistance-temperature relationship of an NTC thermistor is nonlinear, and its sensitivity varies with temperature. It generally has higher relative sensitivity at lower temperatures, while its relative sensitivity tends to decrease as temperature rises. Linear PTC Thermistors: Silicon-based linear PTC thermistors typically exhibit a more uniform resistance change with temperature, helping maintain a consistent measurement response across a relatively wide temperature range. It is important to note that the final measurement resolution depends not only on the thermistor itself but also on the ADC resolution, reference voltage, signal noise, and external circuit design. Linearization: Simplifying Circuit Design Ideally, a sensor's output signal should have a linear relationship with the measured temperature. This simplifies subsequent data processing and temperature conversion. Challenges with NTC Thermistors: The resistance-temperature (R-T) relationship of an NTC thermistor is strongly nonlinear. To improve measurement linearity over the operating temperature range, software compensation is commonly used. Alternatively, additional components, such as a parallel resistor, can be added to the circuit for hardware linearization. Both approaches introduce some additional design or computational complexity. Figure 5. Improving the linearity of an NTC measurement circuit by adding a parallel resistor Advantages of Linear PTC Thermistors: Silicon-based linear PTC thermistors have an inherently more linear R-T characteristic, which can reduce the need for nonlinear compensation and simplify temperature conversion. However, the actual linearity of the output voltage relative to temperature also depends on the excitation circuit design. Figure 6. Linear PTC thermistors do not require a parallel resistor Self-Heating and Long-Term Drift Self-Heating: When current flows through a thermistor, Joule heating occurs, causing the device's own temperature to rise above the surrounding ambient temperature. This can introduce errors into temperature measurements. The degree of self-heating depends on the excitation method and the device's thermal dissipation conditions. For example, under constant-current excitation, thermistor power dissipation is: P = I² × R For an NTC thermistor, resistance decreases as temperature rises, so its power dissipation also decreases under constant-current excitation. Under constant-voltage excitation, however, power dissipation is: P = V² / R In this case, a decrease in NTC resistance may cause power dissipation to increase. Therefore, the excitation current or voltage should be properly controlled to prevent self-heating from affecting measurement accuracy. Long-Term Drift: Long-term drift refers to changes in a thermistor's resistance-temperature characteristics after prolonged operation or exposure to environmental factors such as temperature and humidity. It is closely related to the material, manufacturing process, operating temperature, and application environment. When selecting a thermistor, check the long-term stability and aging test data provided in its datasheet. This is particularly important in applications with demanding reliability requirements, such as automotive electronics and industrial control systems. Calibration All temperature sensors may exhibit component-to-component variations and system-level errors. Therefore, calibration is often necessary in applications requiring high measurement accuracy. NTC Thermistors: Because of their nonlinear R-T characteristics and potentially varying resistance errors across different temperatures, two-point or multipoint calibration may be required in applications with a wide temperature range or strict accuracy requirements. Linear PTC Thermistors: Thanks to their relatively linear characteristics, some devices can achieve good measurement accuracy with single-point calibration. However, multipoint calibration may still be necessary when high accuracy is required across the entire operating temperature range. The appropriate calibration method should be determined based on the required accuracy, operating temperature range, and device datasheet. 4. Software Processing: Converting Voltage into Temperature After the MCU reads the ADC value corresponding to V_TEMP, an algorithm is needed to convert it into an actual temperature value. Two common methods are used. Lookup Table Method A lookup table is created in advance to establish the relationship between resistance or ADC values and temperature. The MCU searches the table using the measured value to obtain the corresponding temperature. Interpolation can also be used to improve conversion accuracy. This method offers fast execution and simple implementation, but it requires additional memory. It is a practical option for MCUs with limited computational resources. Equation-Based Calculation Mathematical models are used to fit the thermistor's R-T curve and convert the measured resistance into temperature. For NTC Thermistors: The Steinhart-Hart equation is commonly used: 1/T = A + B*ln(R) + C*[ln(R)]³ Where T is the absolute temperature in Kelvin (K), R is the thermistor resistance, and A, B, and C are coefficients determined by the device's characteristics. For Linear PTC Thermistors: If the device has a sufficiently linear resistance-temperature relationship, a simple linear equation can be used: T = T₀ + (R − R₀) / (α × R₀) Where T₀ is the reference temperature, R₀ is the resistance at that temperature, and α is the temperature coefficient. For applications requiring higher accuracy, polynomial fitting or lookup tables can also be used to compensate for deviations from ideal linearity. 5. PCB Layout Considerations for Thermistor Circuits Selecting the right thermistor and designing an appropriate measurement circuit are only part of the process. PCB layout also has a direct impact on temperature measurement accuracy. In precision temperature-sensing applications, sensor placement, signal routing, and grounding all require careful consideration. Proper Thermistor Placement The thermistor's position should be determined by the actual temperature measurement target. If the thermistor is used to monitor the temperature of a MOSFET, power resistor, or power management IC, it should be placed as close as practical to the target heat-generating component to minimize temperature differences caused by thermal conduction paths. If it is used for ambient temperature sensing, it should be kept away from power components, heatsinks, and other significant heat sources to prevent localized heating from affecting the readings. Avoid unnecessary large copper areas or other thermally conductive structures that may transfer heat from nearby components to the thermistor, unless these structures are intentionally part of the thermal sensing design. Optimize Analog Signal Routing The output of a thermistor measurement circuit is an analog signal, which can be affected by electromagnetic interference and noise from other circuits. Keep the signal path between the thermistor and the MCU ADC input as short as practical. Avoid routing the signal parallel to high-frequency clock lines, switching nodes, or high-current traces over long distances. If necessary, add an appropriate RC filter at the ADC input to suppress high-frequency noise. Consider Grounding and ADC Reference Voltage Grounding and reference voltage stability also affect temperature measurement accuracy. Avoid sharing long ground paths between the thermistor measurement circuit and high-current return paths to reduce errors caused by ground potential variations. Ensure that the ADC reference voltage is stable to prevent power supply noise from affecting conversion results. For voltage divider measurement circuits, consider using a ratiometric measurement approach in which the divider supply and ADC reference voltage are the same. This helps reduce errors caused by supply voltage fluctuations. 6. Summary and Thermistor Selection Guide NTC and linear PTC thermistors each have their own advantages. The appropriate choice depends on the measurement temperature range, accuracy requirements, cost, and circuit design complexity. Key Selection Considerations: If cost is a major concern and the measurement range is relatively narrow with moderate accuracy requirements, a traditional NTC thermistor is still an excellent choice. It offers low cost, mature technology, and a wide range of available components. However, its nonlinear characteristics and potential temperature compensation requirements should be taken into account. If an application requires better temperature linearity, stable performance across the operating temperature range, and simpler signal processing, a silicon-based linear PTC thermistor may be worth considering. Its relatively linear characteristics can simplify temperature conversion, but the actual measurement accuracy, operating range, and calibration requirements must still be evaluated based on the specific device specifications. In practical designs, thermistor measurement performance depends not only on the sensor itself but also on the excitation circuit, ADC configuration, sensor placement, and thermistor PCB layout. By considering component selection, circuit design, and PCB layout together, designers can develop more accurate and reliable temperature monitoring systems.
