events.before: Resources / 3D Printing Design / 3D Printing in Prosthetics: History, Benefits, and Materials 3D Printing in Prosthetics: History, Benefits, and Materials Written by Dean McClements 6 min read Published August 8, 2022 Updated November 19, 2026 Learn how the use of 3D printing is changing the field of prosthetics. Prosthetics 3D printing is the use of 3D printers to design and create artificial, wearable body parts such as legs, hands, and arms. It is a relatively new method compared to the traditional method of production. The materials used in creating 3D printed prosthetics are accessible and lightweight, making the process suitable for producing prosthetics and providing a favorable alternative for patients worldwide. This article will further discuss 3D printing in prosthetics, how it is used, its history, cost, and benefits. What Is 3D Printing in Prosthetics? Prosthetics 3D printing is the use of additive manufacturing technologies rather than traditional subtractive manufacturing methods to create artificial body parts. These body parts may have been lost through traumatic events or congenital disorders (present at birth). In some cases, amputation surgery may be necessary when a victim's limb or limbs are affected severely by a disease that leads to its atrophy and decomposition (gangrene). In any case, 3D-printed prosthetics serve as a replacement for the missing limbs. For more information, see our guide on 3D printing . You can also explore 3D printing in medicine and healthcare . How is 3D Printing Used in Prosthetics? 3D printing has proven useful in creating prosthetics for a number of reasons. Using 3D printing to fabricate prosthetics leads to a considerable reduction in the manufacturing time, cost, and weight of prosthetics. Prosthetics produced by traditional methods require stringent procedures and are expensive. A prosthetic arm is usually more than $2,000, and the amputee may need to wait for long periods (between 3–6 weeks) for production and delivery to take place. Prosthetics 3D printing, on the other hand, is affordable, has a short lead time, and the required materials are readily available. A 3D-printed arm can cost $395 and be produced in one day. When was the First 3D Printed Prosthetic Created? Efforts were made by scientists and medics to create 3D printed prosthetics from 1990 to 1999. There was a breakthrough as their research saw the creation of the first 3D dental implants and organs. However, 3D printed prosthetic arms, fingers, hands, or legs were still a subject of exploration. Finally, in 2011, a prototype of a 3D printed prosthetic hand was created. Who Created the First 3D Printed Prosthetics? American artist, Ivan Owen, created the first 3D-printed prosthetic in 2011. A 3D printed prosthetic was not his first creation though—it was a mechanical hand. He created this for a steampunk convention and posted a video online of the crafting process. After another collaboration with a carpenter amputee, the project caught the attention of a mother. Her son needed an artificial hand, and prosthetics then were expensive. Owen got to know about her and requested that a 3D printer manufacturing company donate two 3D printers. His request was granted and he created the first 3D-printed prosthetic hand. The issue of the son outgrowing the prosthetic wasn't much of a problem because the printed hand allows for scalability. What are the Most Common 3D Printed Prosthetics? The most common 3D printed prosthetics are: 3D Printed Prosthetic Hand: Prosthetic hands are made for people who have suffered the loss of a limb from the wrist. E-nable prosthetics, an association that oversees a network of makers, enthusiasts, or humanitarians, create different 3D models of prosthetics hands. Some of these models are printed and donated to hundreds of people across the world. 3D Printed Prosthetic Arm: Prosthetic arms can be a combination of a hand and forearm, or a hand, arm, and forearm. Hero prosthetics are acknowledged as the first clinically-approved 3D printed prosthetic arm. Among its functionalities are high five, grab, thumbs up, and pitch. It is aesthetically pleasing and loved especially by children because of the variety of super action figures it represents. The myoelectric functionality makes it possible for the user to have a certain level of control over their 3D printed arm prosthetic. 3D Printed Prosthetic Foot: Prosthetic feet allow users to walk. These are usually made with either elastic heel configurations or solid ankle cushioned heels (SACH). Upya by Exoneo is an affordable, dynamic, and fully biomechanical prosthetic foot that copies the actual anatomy of the toes, ankle, and heel. This allows users to experience the same feeling as a natural foot. For more information, check out our online 3D printing service for your needs. Is it Safe to Use 3D Printed Prosthetics? Yes, it is safe to use 3D printed prosthetics, if the right specifications and product quality are met. The strength and quality of the materials used in the build process will be the basis for measuring the safety of 3D printed prosthetics. Incorrect materials usually break easily because of their inability to bear or sustain the weight of the user. What are the Benefits of 3D Printed Prosthetics? Prosthetic 3D printing offers many benefits compared to its conventional counterpart. One main benefit is the scaling and alignment option of the 3D printed models. Another is the cost and time efficiency it offers as well as the material availability. What are the Materials Used in 3D Printed Prosthetics? The materials used in 3D printed prosthetics are those that are durable and lightweight such as plastic. As an added benefit, the internal structure comprises lightweight materials: carbon fiber, titanium, or aluminum. An artificial prosthetic weight will generally depend on the type of prosthetic and the constituent material. An above-the-knee 3D printed prosthetic weighs about 1.54 kgs, while its traditional counterpart averages 3.62 kgs. How Long do 3D Printed Prosthetics Last? A prosthetic that has been properly manufactured will last for about 3–5 years. A child who is fast-growing, however, would require replacements from time to time. This is because the body part to which the item attaches would have outgrown the 3D printed prosthetic. Are 3D Printed Prosthetics Expensive? No, 3D printed prosthetics are not expensive – especially when compared to traditional prosthetics. You can get a working 3D printed prosthetic for $395. The conventional types are usually sold for thousands of dollars. How Much do 3D Printed Prosthetics Cost? 3D printed prosthetics are generally cost-effective but some high-end designs are expensive. The Hero 3D printed prosthetic arm, created by Open Bionics, for example, has a price range of $10,000-$20,000. It is somewhat cheaper than the conventional bionic prosthetic arm, however. Some charitable organizations<dynamic-value> Kinetic - founded by Mat Bowtell, and Free 3D Hands - have distributed free 3D printed prosthetic arms to many. They have also created assembly manuals for those who wish to create their own prosthetics at home. A notable online marketplace for the purchase of 3D printed prosthetics is Indiamart. What is the Future of 3D Printed Prosthetics? 3D printed prosthetics are still in their infancy stage but have great potential. However, it may be wrong to assume that the technology will completely replace its traditional counterpart. Moreover, a major factor to consider is its acceptance in the medical industry. The first 3D printed bionic arm is clinically-approved; as such when regulatory authorities show interest and give their approval, prosthetic 3D printing will become more entrenched in society. events.before: Resources / 3D Printing Design / ABS vs. PETG: Differences and Comparison ABS vs. PETG: Differences and Comparison Written by Megan Conniff Updated by Dr. Mahder Tewolde PhD 22 min read Published July 27, 2022 Updated November 4, 2026 ABS vs. PETG reveals clear differences in mechanical properties, heat resistance, printability, and outdoor suitability. ABS delivers higher rigidity, impact resistance, and load-bearing strength, supporting demanding mechanical applications and functional components. PETG provides greater flexibility and layer bonding, which reduces cracking under stress and improves part consistency. Heat resistance favors ABS, since ABS maintains structural stability near 100°C, while PETG softens at lower temperatures around 70°C to 80°C. Printability favors PETG due to lower warping, stronger layer adhesion, and reduced sensitivity to thermal contraction during cooling. ABS requires higher extrusion temperatures, controlled environments, and heated enclosures to maintain dimensional accuracy. PETG is more resistant to UV and moisture than ABS but still degrades in prolonged outdoor exposure. PETG maintains appearance and strength longer in mild outdoor conditions. The ABS vs. PETG demonstrates that ABS excels in strength and heat resistance, while PETG offers better printability and outdoor durability. ABS Definition and Comparison to PETG ABS is a strong and durable thermoplastic polymer, recognized for its toughness and impact resistance. ABS is used in applications where strength and resilience are essential, such as automotive parts, toys, and appliances. Petroleum-based ABS offers excellent mechanical properties, including high heat resistance, making it ideal for products exposed to harsh environments. PETG (Polyethylene Terephthalate Glycol) has good chemical resistance and clarity, but “superior” depends on the comparison baseline. PETG is used in the production of containers, signage, and medical devices due to its strength, flexibility, and ease of fabrication. The primary difference between ABS and PETG lies in their chemical resistance and ease of printing. ABS is more prone to warping during 3D printing and generally requires a heated bed to prevent issues, while PETG exhibits less warping and provides better layer adhesion, making it easier to print with fewer failures. PETG provides better moisture resistance and chemical stability, while ABS offers superior impact strength and heat resistance. PETG is more suitable for applications requiring clarity, while ABS is preferred in environments that demand greater durability and resistance to physical stress. The differences make ABS and PETG suitable for distinct applications, with ABS being ideal for structural parts and PETG excelling in applications where flexibility and transparency are essential. The ABS definition refers to Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene, a material known for its toughness, impact resistance, and high heat resistance. "The comparison between ABS and PETG shows that they serve different priorities in functional 3D printing rather than competing directly. ABS remains the stronger choice for high-temperature and load-bearing applications, but it demands tighter process control and more demanding print conditions. PETG trades some heat resistance for easier printability, stronger layer adhesion, and better performance in humid or mildly outdoor environments. Together, the materials illustrate how application requirements, rather than raw strength alone, should guide filament selection." Dr. Mahder Tewolde PhD What are the Advantages of ABS Compared to PETG? The advantages of ABS compared to PETG are listed below. Post-Processing Friendly : ABS offers excellent post-processing capabilities, including easy sanding, painting, and gluing. The smooth surface finish makes it ideal for detailed finishing techniques. Cost-Effective : ABS is more affordable compared to PETG, making it a more economical choice for large-scale manufacturing or production runs. High-Temperature Resistance : ABS exhibits superior heat resistance, withstanding temperatures up to 100°C. ABS maintains its mechanical properties at higher temperatures, making it suitable for automotive and industrial applications. Dimensional Stability : ABS provides dimensional stability in controlled environments (heated bed + enclosure), which helps minimize warping and improve accuracy when a heated bed is used. Transparency : PETG provides excellent clarity, making it ideal for applications requiring transparency (food packaging or medical device components), where visibility and cleanliness are essential. Environmental Resistance : PETG is more resistant to moisture and UV degradation compared to ABS, making it a better choice for outdoor applications or parts exposed to humid environments. Lower Strength : PETG's flexibility is not matched by its mechanical strength or rigidity, as with ABS. Overheating During Printing : PETG has a higher tendency to overheat and produce stringing during the 3D printing process. ABS vs. PETG: Applications Comparison ABS vs. PETG for application comparison highlights the distinct advantages of each material based on their properties. ABS is used in automotive parts, toys, and household appliances due to its strength, impact resistance, and higher heat tolerance. PETG is preferred in medical devices, can be used in food-safe applications if certified, but most 3D printing PETG is not food safe, and structural parts require clarity, flexibility, and good chemical resistance. ABS is more suited for applications demanding durability under stress and higher operating temperatures. PETG excels in environments where moisture or chemical exposure is prevalent and offers better resistance to sunlight (UV) than ABS. The differences inform material selection for specific use cases based on performance requirements. ABS vs. PETG: Part Accuracy Comparison ABS vs. PETG for part accuracy reveals clear differences in dimensional accuracy and layer adhesion. ABS tends to shrink as it cools after printing, which can lead to warping and changes in part dimensions, making it more difficult to meet stringent tolerance requirements. PETG exhibits better layer adhesion and less shrinkage during cooling, resulting in parts that maintain dimensions more consistently. The reduced warping of PETG contributes to higher dimensional stability and better overall part accuracy for larger prints or designs with tight specifications. PETG is a more reliable choice when high precision and consistency are critical because of its characteristics. ABS vs. PETG: Speed Comparison ABS vs. PETG for speed comparison highlights the differences in printing efficiency. ABS and PETG typically print in the 40–60 mm/s range for best results. High-end machines may push PETG faster, but it's not standard. ABS requires higher printing temperatures, around 230 °C to 250 °C, and a heated print bed to prevent warping, which can slow setups. PETG uses elevated extrusion temperatures (around 220 °C to 260 °C) and a heated bed, but its lower susceptibility to warping and better layer adhesion contribute to fewer print failures and more efficient print cycles. ABS vs. PETG: Surface Comparison ABS vs. PETG for surface comparison highlights the differences in finish and smoothness. ABS can produce a reasonably smooth surface when printed correctly, but it is more prone to warping and layer delamination than PETG, which can lead to visible surface imperfections on larger parts. PETG offers better layer adhesion and reduced warping, resulting in more consistent surface quality and fewer visible lines. PETG’s natural clarity and smooth finish make it suitable for parts where a polished or semi‑transparent appearance is desired. PETG requires less surface refinement to achieve a visually appealing part, while ABS surface quality can be improved through post‑processing (such as acetone smoothing). ABS vs. PETG: Heat Resistance ABS vs. PETG for heat resistance reveals key differences in performance under elevated temperatures. ABS has a glass transition temperature of ~105 °C, but mechanical strength begins to degrade below this point, especially under load. PETG typically begins to soften around 75–85 °C, with deformation occurring earlier under mechanical stress. ABS’s higher working temperature tolerance makes it a more appropriate choice for parts subjected to sustained heat. PETG’s lower heat resistance makes it more suitable for applications that do not experience prolonged high temperatures, while offering good performance in moderate thermal environments. ABS vs. PETG: Biodegradability Comparison ABS vs. PETG for biodegradability comparison shows clear differences in environmental impact. ABS and PETG are non‑biodegradable thermoplastics that persist in the environment under natural conditions and do not break down easily. The two materials are recyclable, though PETG is easier to recycle in practice. The recyclability of PETG helps reduce its environmental footprint when processed by appropriate recycling systems, while ABS recycling may require more specialized facilities. Neither ABS nor PETG is biodegradable; both are non‑biodegradable petroleum‑based thermoplastics, but PETG has a stronger recycling pathway, which is preferable for end-of-life handling. ABS vs. PETG: Toxicity Comparison ABS vs. PETG for toxicity comparison reveals differences in material safety during production and use. ABS releases strong, potentially toxic fumes when heated during 3D printing, making good ventilation or air filtration systems essential for safe operation. PETG produces fumes that are not as strong or hazardous as ABS’s emissions, though exposure to volatile organic compounds (VOCs) must be minimized in any printing environment. Printing it in enclosed spaces or home settings presents lower risks compared to ABS, which is considered more problematic without adequate ventilation because PETG’s emissions are less intense. PETG’s lower emission profile makes it a safer choice for indoor applications where exposure to fumes must be reduced. ABS filament is generally less expensive than PETG filament, making it a more economical choice when material cost is a priority, particularly for larger runs or volume printing. Lower ABS material cost reduces upfront expenses, especially for parts that require strength and higher temperature performance without premium pricing. PETG filament is typically priced higher, reflecting its broader versatility, chemical resistance, and easier printing characteristics. PETG’s printing ease and lower risk of failures can reduce indirect costs related to setup and reprints, even if its raw material cost per part is higher. ABS provides cost advantages where budget constraints and mechanical performance are key factors, while PETG’s higher price corresponds with its balanced performance features. Is PETG Stronger Than ABS? No, PETG has higher impact resistance than ABS in many cases, but ABS is stronger under compression and heat. ABS is more rigid and durable under stress, making it better suited for high-stress applications, while PETG offers good strength and flexibility. PETG is typically more impact-resistant and ductile; ABS can crack under impact, making it ideal for automotive parts and heavy-duty functional components. PETG is more flexible and less prone to breaking under tension, but its strength under compression or impact does not match that of ABS. The difference in mechanical properties makes ABS the better choice for high-stress applications, while PETG is preferred in areas requiring flexibility and chemical resistance. Is PETG Heat Resistant Compared to ABS? No, PETG is not as heat-resistant as ABS. PETG handles temperatures up to 70-80°C before it begins to soften or deform, making it more suitable for moderate heat environments, while ABS maintains its structural integrity up to around 100°C. The difference in heat tolerance makes ABS the better choice for parts exposed to elevated temperatures (automotive components or electrical housings). PETG is more suitable for applications where moderate heat resistance is sufficient, such as in food packaging or consumer products. Is PETG UV Resistant? No, PETG is not highly UV resistant. PETG is prone to degradation over time when exposed to prolonged sunlight, while it offers better UV stability than many other plastics. PETG can lose its strength, color, and clarity when exposed to ultraviolet rays, making it less suitable for outdoor applications without additional protective coatings. Materials like ABS, though not UV-resistant in the strictest sense, ABS performs worse than PETG in UV exposure unless specially treated. PETG is better suited for indoor applications or environments with minimal UV exposure. PETG can be treated with UV stabilizers or coatings for improved UV resistance in outdoor applications. What is the PETG vs ABS for Outdoor Use PETG vs ABS for outdoor use shows clear differences in UV resistance and weathering. PETG generally has better UV resistance than ABS, though neither is truly UV‑resistant without additives, making it more vulnerable to degradation when exposed to prolonged sunlight. PETG’s UV stability is limited, causing it to degrade over time, resulting in fading, brittleness, and loss of strength, while the two materials offer some resistance to weathering. ABS performs poorly outdoors unless UV‑stabilized; ASA is the ABS‑derived material designed for outdoor UV exposure. ABS is rarely used unmodified for outdoor exposure; it requires coatings, stabilizers, or replacement with ASA. PETG is better suited for indoor use or applications with minimal UV exposure unless treated with a protective coating. What are the Mutual Alternatives to ABS and PETG? Nylon : Nylon is a versatile thermoplastic material known for its excellent impact resistance, flexibility, and durability, which makes it comparable to ABS and PETG in many applications, but with superior abrasion resistance. Nylon performs well in FDM 3D printing for parts that require strength and wear resistance. The material is highly resistant to abrasion and has good chemical resistance, making it suitable for functional parts such as gears, bearings, and automotive components. Polycarbonate : Polycarbonate is another alternative with outstanding impact resistance and strength. Polycarbonate offers better heat resistance than ABS and PETG, making it ideal for high-performance applications. The material is used in applications that require transparency, high strength, and toughness (protective covers, optical lenses, and electrical housings). What are the Similarities Between ABS and PETG? The similarities between ABS and PETG are listed below. Non-Biodegradable : ABS and PETG are non-biodegradable, meaning the materials do not naturally break down in the environment and can contribute to long-term pollution if not correctly disposed of. Susceptibility to Moisture : ABS and PETG are susceptible to moisture absorption, which can affect their printing properties, though PETG has better moisture resistance compared to ABS. ABS and PETG need to be kept dry during storage to prevent issues such as bubbling or weak layers. High-Temperature Printing : ABS and PETG are used in 3D printing processes that require high extrusion temperatures. The materials are compatible with printers that operate at elevated temperatures, ranging from 220°C to 250°C, to ensure proper melting and layer bonding. Recyclability : ABS and PETG are recyclable, which allows them to be reprocessed and reused in the production of new products. Recycling the materials reduces waste and their environmental impact when handled properly through recycling systems. What are Other Comparisons for ABS Besides PETG? The other comparison for ABS, besides PETG, is listed below. ABS vs. PLA : PLA (polylactic acid) is a biodegradable plastic that is more rigid than ABS, though it is weaker and more brittle. PLA is easier to print and is well-suited for hobbyist projects due to its lower heat resistance, while ABS has better durability and impact resistance. High-temperature applications make PLA unsuitable for parts that are exposed to heat. Toughness is not due to weight difference; it's due to material ductility and impact resistance. ABS vs. ASA : ASA (Acrylonitrile styrene-acrylate) is a high-performance plastic similar to ABS, used in applications requiring high strength. ASA has superior UV resistance, making it better for outdoor use compared to ABS, which degrades under sunlight exposure. The cost of ASA is higher than that of ABS, but it is durable, impact-resistant, and weather-resistant, making it ideal for applications in outdoor environments ( automotive and outdoor signage). What are Other Comparisons for PETG Besides ABS? The other comparisons for PETG besides ABS are listed below. PETG vs. PET : PETG is derived from PET by replacing the glycol molecule with a larger monomer, resulting in better shock resistance and higher temperature tolerance. PETG provides improved impact resistance and flexibility, making it more suitable for applications requiring toughness and flexibility, while PET has similar or slightly better heat resistance but is more prone to crystallization, making it harder to print. PETG vs. TPU : PETG is tougher but less flexible than TPU (thermoplastic polyurethane). TPU is more flexible and suitable for applications that require elasticity, such as phone cases or wearable parts. A more rigid PETG is better suited to applications requiring strength and clarity. PETG needs a heated bed temperature between 60°C and 80°C, while TPU typically prints at 210–240 °C; 40–60 °C refers to the heated bed, not the nozzle, making TPU easier to print in some cases. The odor can be problematic in poorly ventilated areas, requiring proper ventilation or air filtration systems to mitigate exposure. The smell may be a concern in enclosed spaces or home environments, making ABS less suitable for printing in areas without adequate airflow or filtration. PETG Definition and Comparison to ABS PETG (Polyethylene Terephthalate Glycol) is a thermoplastic polyester known for its strength, flexibility, and resistance to impact. The material is a popular choice in 3D printing due to its ease of use, minimal warping, and durability. PETG offers excellent chemical resistance and high moisture resistance, making it suitable for applications involving exposure to water or various chemicals. PETG has a lower tendency to warp during printing, making it easier to work with compared to ABS. PETG offers superior flexibility, transparency, and better resistance to environmental factors like moisture, while ABS is stronger in terms of impact resistance and high-temperature performance. PETG is used in medical devices, food packaging, and structural parts for its clarity and chemical stability. ABS is preferred for automotive parts, electronics, and toys requiring higher strength and heat resistance. What are the Advantages of PETG Compared to ABS? The advantages of PETG compared to ABS are listed below. Ease of Printing : PETG is easier to print than ABS, with less warping and fewer adhesion issues. The lower printing temperatures and heated bed make it more suitable for 3D printing. Chemical Resistance : PETG offers better chemical resistance than ABS in specific environments, especially to oils, moisture, and some chemicals, increasing its durability in specific industrial applications. Flexibility : PETG is more flexible and ductile but typically has lower impact resistance than ABS. Transparency : PETG provides excellent clarity, making it ideal for applications requiring transparency (food packaging or medical device components), where visibility and cleanliness are essential. Environmental Resistance : PETG is more resistant to moisture and UV degradation compared to ABS, making it a better choice for outdoor applications or parts exposed to humid environments. What are the Disadvantages of PETG Compared to ABS? The disadvantages of PETG compared to ABS are listed below. Lower Heat Resistance : PETG has lower heat resistance compared to ABS, withstanding temperatures up to 70-80°C, which makes it less suitable for applications exposed to higher temperatures. PETG is ideal for moderate heat environments (some electronics and consumer products). Surface Scratching : PETG is more prone to surface scratches than ABS when used in high-contact applications. The material lacks the same level of hardness as ABS, which limits its durability for items subjected to rough handling or wear. Lower Strength : PETG's flexibility is not matched by its mechanical strength or rigidity, as with ABS. Applications requiring high structural integrity or impact resistance may suffer from a disadvantage under heavy loads. Overheating During Printing : PETG has a higher tendency to overheat and produce stringing during the 3D printing process. The issue can lead to messy prints, requiring careful temperature control and fine-tuning during the printing process to avoid excessive oozing. Difficulty in Post-Processing : PETG is more challenging to post-process than ABS when it comes to sanding and painting. The material’s smooth surface can be more rigid to work with, which may limit its ability to be easily modified for specific applications. Comparison Table Between ABS and PETG Comparison between ABS and PETG is shown in the table below. ABS vs. PETG: Applications Comparison ABS vs. PETG for application comparison highlights the distinct advantages of each material based on their properties. ABS is used in automotive parts, toys, and household appliances due to its strength, impact resistance, and higher heat tolerance. PETG is preferred in medical devices, can be used in food-safe applications if certified, but most 3D printing PETG is not food safe, and structural parts require clarity, flexibility, and good chemical resistance. ABS is more suited for applications demanding durability under stress and higher operating temperatures. PETG excels in environments where moisture or chemical exposure is prevalent and offers better resistance to sunlight (UV) than ABS. The differences inform material selection for specific use cases based on performance requirements. ABS vs. PETG: Part Accuracy Comparison ABS vs. PETG for part accuracy reveals clear differences in dimensional accuracy and layer adhesion. ABS tends to shrink as it cools after printing, which can lead to warping and changes in part dimensions, making it more difficult to meet stringent tolerance requirements. PETG exhibits better layer adhesion and less shrinkage during cooling, resulting in parts that maintain dimensions more consistently. The reduced warping of PETG contributes to higher dimensional stability and better overall part accuracy for larger prints or designs with tight specifications. PETG is a more reliable choice when high precision and consistency are critical because of its characteristics. ABS vs. PETG: Speed Comparison ABS vs. PETG for speed comparison highlights the differences in printing efficiency. ABS and PETG typically print in the 40–60 mm/s range for best results. High-end machines may push PETG faster, but it's not standard. ABS requires higher printing temperatures, around 230 °C to 250 °C, and a heated print bed to prevent warping, which can slow setups. PETG uses elevated extrusion temperatures (around 220 °C to 260 °C) and a heated bed, but its lower susceptibility to warping and better layer adhesion contribute to fewer print failures and more efficient print cycles. ABS vs. PETG: Surface Comparison ABS vs. PETG for surface comparison highlights the differences in finish and smoothness. ABS can produce a reasonably smooth surface when printed correctly, but it is more prone to warping and layer delamination than PETG, which can lead to visible surface imperfections on larger parts. PETG offers better layer adhesion and reduced warping, resulting in more consistent surface quality and fewer visible lines. PETG’s natural clarity and smooth finish make it suitable for parts where a polished or semi‑transparent appearance is desired. PETG requires less surface refinement to achieve a visually appealing part, while ABS surface quality can be improved through post‑processing (such as acetone smoothing). ABS vs. PETG: Heat Resistance ABS vs. PETG for heat resistance reveals key differences in performance under elevated temperatures. ABS has a glass transition temperature of ~105 °C, but mechanical strength begins to degrade below this point, especially under load. PETG typically begins to soften around 75–85 °C, with deformation occurring earlier under mechanical stress. ABS’s higher working temperature tolerance makes it a more appropriate choice for parts subjected to sustained heat. PETG’s lower heat resistance makes it more suitable for applications that do not experience prolonged high temperatures, while offering good performance in moderate thermal environments. ABS vs. PETG: Biodegradability Comparison ABS vs. PETG for biodegradability comparison shows clear differences in environmental impact. ABS and PETG are non‑biodegradable thermoplastics that persist in the environment under natural conditions and do not break down easily. The two materials are recyclable, though PETG is easier to recycle in practice. The recyclability of PETG helps reduce its environmental footprint when processed by appropriate recycling systems, while ABS recycling may require more specialized facilities. Neither ABS nor PETG is biodegradable; both are non‑biodegradable petroleum‑based thermoplastics, but PETG has a stronger recycling pathway, which is preferable for end-of-life handling. ABS vs. PETG: Toxicity Comparison ABS vs. PETG for toxicity comparison reveals differences in material safety during production and use. ABS releases strong, potentially toxic fumes when heated during 3D printing, making good ventilation or air filtration systems essential for safe operation. PETG produces fumes that are not as strong or hazardous as ABS’s emissions, though exposure to volatile organic compounds (VOCs) must be minimized in any printing environment. Printing it in enclosed spaces or home settings presents lower risks compared to ABS, which is considered more problematic without adequate ventilation because PETG’s emissions are less intense. PETG’s lower emission profile makes it a safer choice for indoor applications where exposure to fumes must be reduced. ABS vs. PETG: Cost Comparison ABS vs. PETG for cost comparison shows clear differences in material pricing and printing expenses. ABS filament is generally less expensive than PETG filament, making it a more economical choice when material cost is a priority, particularly for larger runs or volume printing. Lower ABS material cost reduces upfront expenses, especially for parts that require strength and higher temperature performance without premium pricing. PETG filament is typically priced higher, reflecting its broader versatility, chemical resistance, and easier printing characteristics. PETG’s printing ease and lower risk of failures can reduce indirect costs related to setup and reprints, even if its raw material cost per part is higher. ABS provides cost advantages where budget constraints and mechanical performance are key factors, while PETG’s higher price corresponds with its balanced performance features. Is PETG Stronger Than ABS? No, PETG has higher impact resistance than ABS in many cases, but ABS is stronger under compression and heat. ABS is more rigid and durable under stress, making it better suited for high-stress applications, while PETG offers good strength and flexibility. PETG is typically more impact-resistant and ductile; ABS can crack under impact, making it ideal for automotive parts and heavy-duty functional components. PETG is more flexible and less prone to breaking under tension, but its strength under compression or impact does not match that of ABS. The difference in mechanical properties makes ABS the better choice for high-stress applications, while PETG is preferred in areas requiring flexibility and chemical resistance. Is PETG Heat Resistant Compared to ABS? No, PETG is not as heat-resistant as ABS. PETG handles temperatures up to 70-80°C before it begins to soften or deform, making it more suitable for moderate heat environments, while ABS maintains its structural integrity up to around 100°C. The difference in heat tolerance makes ABS the better choice for parts exposed to elevated temperatures (automotive components or electrical housings). PETG is more suitable for applications where moderate heat resistance is sufficient, such as in food packaging or consumer products. Is PETG UV Resistant? No, PETG is not highly UV resistant. PETG is prone to degradation over time when exposed to prolonged sunlight, while it offers better UV stability than many other plastics. PETG can lose its strength, color, and clarity when exposed to ultraviolet rays, making it less suitable for outdoor applications without additional protective coatings. Materials like ABS, though not UV-resistant in the strictest sense, ABS performs worse than PETG in UV exposure unless specially treated. PETG is better suited for indoor applications or environments with minimal UV exposure. PETG can be treated with UV stabilizers or coatings for improved UV resistance in outdoor applications. What is the PETG vs ABS for Outdoor Use PETG vs ABS for outdoor use shows clear differences in UV resistance and weathering. PETG generally has better UV resistance than ABS, though neither is truly UV‑resistant without additives, making it more vulnerable to degradation when exposed to prolonged sunlight. PETG’s UV stability is limited, causing it to degrade over time, resulting in fading, brittleness, and loss of strength, while the two materials offer some resistance to weathering. ABS performs poorly outdoors unless UV‑stabilized; ASA is the ABS‑derived material designed for outdoor UV exposure. ABS is rarely used unmodified for outdoor exposure; it requires coatings, stabilizers, or replacement with ASA. PETG is better suited for indoor use or applications with minimal UV exposure unless treated with a protective coating. What are the Mutual Alternatives to ABS and PETG? The mutual alternatives to ABS and PETG are listed below. Nylon : Nylon is a versatile thermoplastic material known for its excellent impact resistance, flexibility, and durability, which makes it comparable to ABS and PETG in many applications, but with superior abrasion resistance. Nylon performs well in FDM 3D printing for parts that require strength and wear resistance. The material is highly resistant to abrasion and has good chemical resistance, making it suitable for functional parts such as gears, bearings, and automotive components. Polycarbonate : Polycarbonate is another alternative with outstanding impact resistance and strength. Polycarbonate offers better heat resistance than ABS and PETG, making it ideal for high-performance applications. The material is used in applications that require transparency, high strength, and toughness (protective covers, optical lenses, and electrical housings). What are the Similarities Between ABS and PETG? The similarities between ABS and PETG are listed below. Non-Biodegradable : ABS and PETG are non-biodegradable, meaning the materials do not naturally break down in the environment and can contribute to long-term pollution if not correctly disposed of. Susceptibility to Moisture : ABS and PETG are susceptible to moisture absorption, which can affect their printing properties, though PETG has better moisture resistance compared to ABS. ABS and PETG need to be kept dry during storage to prevent issues such as bubbling or weak layers. High-Temperature Printing : ABS and PETG are used in 3D printing processes that require high extrusion temperatures. The materials are compatible with printers that operate at elevated temperatures, ranging from 220°C to 250°C, to ensure proper melting and layer bonding. Recyclability : ABS and PETG are recyclable, which allows them to be reprocessed and reused in the production of new products. Recycling the materials reduces waste and their environmental impact when handled properly through recycling systems. What are Other Comparisons for ABS Besides PETG? The other comparison for ABS, besides PETG, is listed below. ABS vs. PLA : PLA (polylactic acid) is a biodegradable plastic that is more rigid than ABS, though it is weaker and more brittle. PLA is easier to print and is well-suited for hobbyist projects due to its lower heat resistance, while ABS has better durability and impact resistance. High-temperature applications make PLA unsuitable for parts that are exposed to heat. Toughness is not due to weight difference; it's due to material ductility and impact resistance. ABS vs. ASA : ASA (Acrylonitrile styrene-acrylate) is a high-performance plastic similar to ABS, used in applications requiring high strength. ASA has superior UV resistance, making it better for outdoor use compared to ABS, which degrades under sunlight exposure. The cost of ASA is higher than that of ABS, but it is durable, impact-resistant, and weather-resistant, making it ideal for applications in outdoor environments ( automotive and outdoor signage). What are Other Comparisons for PETG Besides ABS? The other comparisons for PETG besides ABS are listed below. PETG vs. PET : PETG is derived from PET by replacing the glycol molecule with a larger monomer, resulting in better shock resistance and higher temperature tolerance. PETG provides improved impact resistance and flexibility, making it more suitable for applications requiring toughness and flexibility, while PET has similar or slightly better heat resistance but is more prone to crystallization, making it harder to print. PETG vs. TPU : PETG is tougher but less flexible than TPU (thermoplastic polyurethane). TPU is more flexible and suitable for applications that require elasticity, such as phone cases or wearable parts. A more rigid PETG is better suited to applications requiring strength and clarity. PETG needs a heated bed temperature between 60°C and 80°C, while TPU typically prints at 210–240 °C; 40–60 °C refers to the heated bed, not the nozzle, making TPU easier to print in some cases. events.before: Resources / 3D Printing Design / Additive vs. Subtractive Manufacturing Comparison Additive vs. Subtractive Manufacturing Comparison Written by Dean McClements 6 min read Published November 1, 2021 Updated November 20, 2026 One of the most important up-front decisions when designing a new product is the choice of manufacturing technology. This is often when the comparison of additive vs. subtractive manufacturing comes into play. This article aims to compare these, highlight the benefits of each, and make suggestions on when to use them. What is Subtractive Manufacturing? Subtractive manufacturing refers to the process of removing material from raw stock supplied in plates, bars, billets, or other bulk forms. Rotating or stationary tools are employed to strip material away until the part takes on the right shape. This is the most common method used to manufacture metal parts, but plastics can also be manufactured using subtractive technologies. The vast majority of modern subtractive machines are CNC-based as manually operated machines cannot compete with the speed and precision of computer-controlled systems. Subtractive Manufacturing Technologies When it comes to additive vs subtractive manufacturing methods, the latter has a wide range of mature technologies that haven’t fundamentally changed over the past few decades. The most common are listed below. 1. Turning Turning is performed on a machine called a lathe. It works by spinning material in a chuck or collet while a stationary tool is introduced into the side of the material. The cutting tool is moved parallel (Z-axis) and perpendicular (X-axis) to the axis of rotation. The tool typically does not move on the Y-axis at all. CNC lathes can simultaneously control a tools’ position along the X and Z axes to create complex geometries. Turning is ideal for cylindrical parts like shafts. There are many different configurations from very simple and cheap lathes to Swiss-style machines that can produce complex multi-feature parts to heavy-duty multi-spindle lathes. 2. Milling Milling works by fixing a billet of raw material in a vice attached to the machine bed while a spinning tool is moved into contact to cut away material. Milling machines can be supplied with 3, 5, or 6 degrees of freedom. More degrees of freedom allow the machine to create more complex features. However, such machines are also more expensive to purchase and operate. Milling machines are ideal for multi-featured flat-faced parts. 3. Profile Cutting Profile cutting is another type of subtractive technology that can create flat parts by cutting out a profile using a beam of energy (plasma or laser) or a high-pressure stream of water (waterjet). Each of these technologies has advantages and disadvantages. For example, waterjets can cut through thicker plates than laser cutters but require a lot more maintenance and auxiliary equipment. 4. Electrical Discharge Machining Electrical discharge machining (EDM) is an advanced subtractive technology that removes material using an electrode to erode material from the part’s surface without ever touching it. This process is also known as spark erosion. EDM can produce highly accurate parts and can cut any conductive metal. The cutting/erosion tool can either be a wire to create profile parts of almost any thickness or a specially shaped electrode to create complex geometries for injection molds. Advantages of Subtractive Manufacturing There is a reason subtractive manufacturing is so common. When comparing additive vs subtractive manufacturing, this more classical method offers the following advantages. 1. Accuracy: Subtractive machines can be extremely accurate when compared to additive ones. Additive parts that need high-accuracy features often need to be machined after printing. 2. Surface Finish: CNC machines can achieve smoother, more precise surface finishes than additive machines. 3. High Production Volume: CNC machines can achieve much higher production rates than additive machines and can be easily set up to automate production runs. Raw material can be automatically loaded into the machine and completed parts can be removed without any human intervention. When it comes to metal additive vs. subtractive manufacturing, the long history of subtractive technologies offers a more well-developed body of manufacturing knowledge. Subtractive is typically a safe bet when manufacturing metal parts. Parts made with additive manufacturing What is Additive Manufacturing? Additive manufacturing, also called 3D printing, refers to the process of manufacturing a part via the addition of material. This contrasts with most traditional methods that involve cutting away (subtracting) portions from a larger piece of raw material. In most additive processes, this is achieved by adding either plastic or metal in a layer-by-layer fashion until the part is complete. Additive technology has matured over the past decade to the point where these machines can be considered for use in actual production and not just for the manufacture of prototypes. Additive Manufacturing Technologies When it comes to additive vs subtractive manufacturing technologies, most additive ones are relatively new, and unique additive methods are constantly being developed. A wide range of different additive techniques is currently available. In general, these can be categorized by the type of material they print. 1. Plastic Additive Manufacturing Plastic additive manufacturing can produce plastic parts using a wide range of different technologies from laser-bonded powder systems like selective laser sintering (SLS) to advanced photopolymerization techniques like stereolithography (SLA) or carbon digital light synthesis (DLS) . Parts can be printed in hard thermoplastics or soft thermosetting polymers . In the contest between plastic additive vs. subtractive manufacturing, additive technologies offer more overall versatility in terms of materials and the ability to manufacture complex multi-material parts. 2. Metal Additive Manufacturing Metal additive manufacturing has come a long way and is now considered a mature technology. There are many different styles but they can be broken down into two subcategories. Powder-based systems use lasers or electron beams to metal powder into a solid part. Fused deposition modeling (FDM) technologies, on the other hand, print the part with metal powder encased in a polymer binder. After the print, the part is fired in a furnace to evaporate the binders and sinter the metal particles together. Advantages of Additive Manufacturing When comparing additive vs subtractive manufacturing, additive manufacturing has many unique advantages such as those below. 1. Easy Setup: Additive manufacturing is quite simple to set up. In most cases, the part can be designed in CAD, digitally sliced (turned into g-code), and printed immediately with a limited setup. 2. Complex Parts: Additive manufacturing can produce parts that are simply impossible on subtractive machines. Hollow or complex internal cavities are easy to make with additive machines but often cannot be achieved with other manufacturing techniques. 3. Rapid Manufacturing: Additive manufacturing can be used to quickly create a one-off part and rapidly iterate through design variations. This is due to the easy setup and the fact that raw material doesn’t need special preparations beforehand. When to use Additive vs. Subtractive Manufacturing Deciding between additive vs. subtractive manufacturing depends on many different factors. Metal additive manufacturing is currently more expensive per part than metal subtractive manufacturing. It is, however, cheaper to 3D print a plastic part than to machine it. When relatively short production runs of complex parts are needed, additive manufacturing is often the best option but subtractive wins out in low-complexity, high-volume situations. Contact a Xometry expert to learn which technology is best suited to your application. Alternatively, use the Xometry quoting tool to get an idea of the cost differences between subtractive vs. additive manufacturing. Ready to Get Your Parts Started? events.before: Resources / 3D Printing Design / Elongation: Definition, How To Calculate, and Importance Elongation: Definition, How To Calculate, and Importance Written by Dean McClements 10 min read Published March 16, 2023 Updated November 10, 2026 Learn more about this type of measurement and what it means in manufacturing. Elongation is the measurable tendency of a material to stretch when under strain. Engineers use a standardized testing procedure and a dumbbell-shaped test sample to evaluate a given material’s characteristic elongation behavior. The sample’s elongation is expressed as a percentage — its increase in length is divided by the original length and multiplied by 100 to calculate this value. Elongation is important because it is a measure of a material’s ductility — its ability to deform without breaking. This is a key measure in 3D-printable materials, as it is relevant to the practical durability of 3D-printed components in real-world applications. This article will define elongation, its importance, and how to calculate it. What Does Elongation Mean? Elongation is the amount that a material permanently lengthens when experiencing a tensile force (strain). It is a numerical measure of the ductility of the material — how easily it deforms under strain. It is measured according to very specific controlled conditions so that the values of elongation can be quantitatively compared between materials. Elongation is specifically measured using a standardized shape of sample material, which is then acted upon by a known pulling force. The length by which the material sample lengthens is measured until the force is great enough to break the sample. What Is Elongation in the Physics of Deformation? Elongation in terms of the physics of deformation is a measure of how much an element lengthens when subjected to tensile stress. It’s expressed as a ratio of the new length to its original length. What Is Elongation in Astronomy? Elongation in astronomy is a measure of the angular separation between a body in the solar system and the sun when viewed from earth. It describes the relative position of planets and other celestial bodies in the solar system, compared to the earth and sun. What Is Elongation in Geometry? Elongation in geometry refers to the stretching of a geometric shape along one or more axes. For example, in a 2-dimensional plane, if a square were to be elongated along one axis, it would become a rectangle. In a 3-dimensional space, if a cube were elongated along a single axis, it would become a rectangular prism. This concept is important in geometric transformations. What Is Elongation in Plasma Physics? Elongation in plasma physics refers to the shape of a fusion plasma. A plasma cloud can be shaped, and the elongation of a particular shape is defined as the ratio of the length of the cloud on its longest axis to the length of its shortest axis. Elongation is an important factor as more elongated plasma clouds tend to be less stable and more difficult to confine. What Is Elongation in Biology? Elongation in biology is a part of the DNA translation process, where proteins are built from RNA that has been transcribed from DNA. More specifically, elongation is the second phase of translation, occurring between the initiation and termination of the process. Elongation refers to the amino acid chain lengthening during translation. How To Calculate the Elongation of a Material? The elongation of a material is calculated according to international testing standards. The most common standard for calculating elongation is ASTM D412. It specifies the shape of the material sample to be used. The shape is called a dumbbell, as it is roughly oblong but with wider ends (for gripping) and a thinner strip in the middle, which will elongate when pulled. The material sample is gripped by a testing machine and a steadily increasing pulling force (strain) is applied to the dumbbell. The testing machine measures how the sample length increases with increasing strain. This data is plotted onto a graph. The elongation is calculated as the amount that the material’s length increased, divided by its original length. This is quoted as a percentage. What Is the Formula of Elongation? The formula for elongation is the deformation (increase in length) of a sample divided by the original length of the sample, multiplied by 100 (to convert to a percentage). Percent Elongation = 100 x ((Final Length - Original Length) / Original Length) Or, written using symbols: Percent Elongation = ɛ = (ΔL/L) x 100 What Is the Unit of Elongation? Elongation is reported as a percent, so it doesn’t technically have a unit. This is because the elongation of a material is a ratio of the material’s change in length when it breaks to the original length of the sample. The ratio is converted to a percentage. What Is the Symbol for Elongation? The symbol for elongation is the lowercase Greek letter ε (epsilon). What Is the Importance of Elongation? Knowledge of elongation is important so you can understand how much a material will deform under strain. It can be used as a measure of ductility. The deformation and ductility of a material are important to know for applications where some deformation is expected, such as in crash barriers. Conversely, elongation is an important factor when designing parts such as door hinges which can accept very little deformation under strain. What Is Elongation in 3D Printing? Elongation in 3D printing is the amount of deformation that a 3D-printed material can withstand before breaking. It is an indication of how durable a 3D-printed item will be. The growing popularity of 3D printing has underscored the poor mechanical strength of many printable materials and technologies (such as FDM or resin). Is Elongation an Important Measure in 3D Printing Materials? Yes, elongation is an important consideration when choosing 3D printing materials, as it provides information about how much the material can deform without breaking. The physical properties of their constituent materials dictate the usefulness of 3D-printed components. Many items must be durable in order to be practical in real-world circumstances. Is There a Device Used in Measuring the Elongation of Materials? Yes, there are specially designed devices for measuring the elongation of materials according to international standards like ASTM D412. These testing systems have a number of components, each of which is intended for certain material tests. Firstly, the device has grips that hold each end of the material dumbbell sample. Secondly, the testing system uses a measuring device called an extensometer to measure the change in the sample’s length as increasing strain is applied. It is also possible to use machines that include environmental chambers. By encasing the grips, material sample, and extensometer, they control the environmental conditions (such as temperature) in order to test under very specific conditions. A number of specialist suppliers manufacture these testing systems for sale to any organization that needs to carry out regular tests according to standards such as ASTM D412. What Are the Different Types of Elongation Measurement? The different types of elongation measurements are as follows: 1. Ductility Ductility is the ability of a material to deform without breaking. Materials that are not ductile are instead called brittle — they deform very little before breaking. The ductility of a material can be inferred by a number of measurements — the most common is percent elongation, but the reduction in area and cupping tests can also be important. 2. Elongation at Break Elongation at break is the measured elongation of a sample of material at the point at which it breaks. Tensile stress is applied to the material sample, causing it to lengthen. As this stress increases, the stretching of the material will first be elastic (can revert to its original position when the stress is released) and then plastic (permanent deformation). If the stress continues to be applied after plastic lengthening occurs, the material will eventually break. The length at this point is the elongation at break , often stated as a percentage lengthening compared to the original length. What Is Percent Elongation? Percent elongation is the percentage that a material stretches beyond its original length before it actually breaks. Elongation is measured as the change in length in a material sample, divided by its original length, multiplied by 100 to convert it to a percentage. How To Calculate the Percent Elongation? Percent elongation is calculated using data from a testing system. First, the material to be tested is cast or machined into a specific dumbbell shape according to the international standard ASTM D412. Second, the dumbbell of material is clamped into the testing machine and a tensile (stretching) force is applied. An extensometer measures the increase in length within the thin section of the dumbbell. This relationship between length and tensile strength can be plotted on a simple graph. The test ends when the dumbbell breaks. Finally, percent elongation is calculated from this data. The change in total length divided by the starting length multiplied by 100 gives the percent elongation. Frequently Asked Questions About Elongation Why Do We Need To Calculate Material Elongation? It is valuable to calculate material elongation so that there is a standardized way to estimate and compare the ductility of different materials. It is important to be able to quantitatively compare different grades on a number of material properties, especially when selecting a specific grade of material for a project. The elongation of a material can be a critical property in certain applications such as crash barriers that need to absorb significant energy before failing. How Does Tensile Strength Relate to Elongation? The relationship between tensile strength and elongation depends on the material. Typically, materials that have high tensile strength tend not to elongate by much — these are materials like ceramics and some tough metals. This means that they will withstand high tensile stress before breaking; however, since they’re brittle, they won’t deform much before that breaking point. That can make the break seem sudden or unexpected. Typically, materials with high elongation values have low tensile strengths. If the material is easily stretched, it often cannot withstand much tensile stress. This includes most polymers plus soft metals like copper. However, there are engineered materials (alloys and composites) that exhibit significant elongation in combination with high tensile strength. These are valuable for specific applications such as structural components that experience high dynamic loads. What Is the Difference Between Elongation and Tensile Strength? Tensile strength indicates how much force the material can withstand, whereas elongation indicates how ductile the material is. Tensile strength is a measure of how much tensile stress (force) can be exerted on a material before it breaks. It is measured in units of force per unit area, such as psi or MPa. Elongation is rather a measure of how much that material will stretch under tensile stress before breaking — its so-called ultimate elongation. It is measured as a percentage change in the sample’s length. To learn more, see our full guide on Tensile Strength . events.before: Resources / 3D Printing Design / PETG vs. PLA: Strength and Printing Comparison PETG vs. PLA: Strength and Printing Comparison Written by Megan Conniff Updated by Audrius Zidonis PhD 11 min read Published July 27, 2022 Updated November 10, 2026 PETG and PLA represent two of the most widely used thermoplastics in fused deposition modeling due to their accessibility, versatility, and compatibility with standard 3D printers. PLA is derived from renewable resources that offer higher biodegradability and lower thermal resistance. PETG is synthesized from petroleum-based compounds and provides greater durability and chemical resilience. PETG exhibits superior impact resistance and toughness, making it suitable for mechanical parts, while PLA maintains higher rigidity and tensile strength, typically between 50 and 70 MPa, with low elongation before break. Ductility differs between the two; PETG undergoes plastic deformation and bends under stress without fracturing, while PLA tends to snap when subjected to similar forces. Heat resistance favors PETG, which retains structural integrity at temperatures up to 70–75 °C, while PLA begins to deform near 50–55 °C. What are the Differences Between PETG and PLA? The differences between PETG and PLA are shown in the table below. Advantage - Superior performance Limitation - Requires consideration Neutral - Standard characteristic Winner - Best in category How much more Flexible is PETG than PLA? PETG is functionally more flexible than PLA because of its higher ductility, which allows it to bend under stress whereas PLA remains rigid. PLA breaks or snaps when subjected to bending forces. PETG deforms and bends before reaching a point of failure. The material properties make PETG suitable for components requiring minor elastic deformation. The elongation at break for PETG remains higher than standard PLA. Is PETG more flexible than PLA? Yes, PETG exhibits greater practical flexibility than PLA. This is due to its superior ductility, which allows it to maintain its integrity through bending and impact. PLA tends to be brittle and shatters under stress. PETG maintains its integrity through bending and impact. What is the Melting Point of PETG compared to PLA? The melting point of PETG ranges between 230°C and 250°C compared to PLA, which melts at around 180°C to 220°C. Higher temperatures remain necessary for PETG to transition into a flowable state. PLA requires lower energy input for extrusion due to its chemical composition. Proper cooling becomes critical for PLA to prevent sagging. Thermal properties dictate the hardware requirements for each material. Printers must achieve a consistent PETG melting temperature. Accurate control is vital for managing the PETG melting point. Which Filament has better Heat Resistance, PLA or PETG? PETG has better heat resistance compared to PLA. PLA begins to soften and deform at temperatures as low as 50°C to 60°C. PETG maintains structural integrity up to 80°C. Automotive interiors or outdoor environments cause PLA parts to fail. Choosing the right material depends on the operating temperature of the final application. Users compare PETG filament vs PLA for functional parts. Environmental conditions influence the choice between PLA vs. PETG filament. Is PETG stronger than PLA? No, PLA is not stronger than PETG. Parts printed in PLA resist stretching more effectively than parts printed in PETG. The PETG offers better impact strength and durability despite its lower tensile rating. PLA parts fail abruptly through cracking. PETG parts tend to bend or deform before breaking. What are the Advantages of PETG Compared to PLA? The advantages of PETG compared to PLA are listed below. Very Flexible : The material withstands significant bending without snapping. Pliability allows for the creation of snap-fit joints and living hinges. Fairly Chemically Stable or Chemical Resistance : PETG resists degradation from various acids, alkalis, and salts. It serves well in environments exposed to cleaning agents or industrial chemicals. High-Impact Strength (Less Likely to Fracture) : Parts absorb energy during collisions without shattering. The characteristics increase the longevity of protective housings and guards. Abrasion-Resistant and Tough : The surface resists wear from friction and mechanical contact. Constant use results in minimal material loss over time. Higher Thermal Stability or Heat Resistance : Components retain their shape in temperatures up to 70°C to 75°C. Stability makes it useful for electronic enclosures that generate heat. Better UV and Weather Resistance : Outdoor exposure does not cause the material to become brittle or discolored quickly. Sunlight has a minimal effect on the structural bonds of the polymer. Water or Moisture Resistance : The plastic behaves as an effective barrier against liquid penetration. It remains stable when submerged or used in humid conditions. Better Layer Adhesion : Molten layers bond together strongly to create a near-isotropic part. Strong bonding reduces the risk of delamination under vertical stress. Glossy Surface Finish : Finished parts exhibit a natural shine that improves aesthetic appeal. Smooth finishes reduce the need for extensive post-processing or painting. Recyclability : The material is technically recyclable but requires dedicated processing streams to avoid contaminating standard PET recycling. Functional Prototype Viability : Real-world testing becomes possible due to the material durability and thermal properties. It bridges the gap between conceptual models and end-use products for Polyethylene Terephthalate Glycol . What are the Disadvantages of PETG Compared to PLA? The disadvantages of PETG compared to PLA are listed below. Stringing and Oozing : High print temperatures cause material to leak from the nozzle during travel moves. Fine wisps of plastic require manual removal after the print completes. Hygroscopic Nature : The filament absorbs moisture from the air rapidly. A saturated filament leads to bubbles, popping sounds, and poor surface quality. Difficulty with Supports : Strong layer adhesion makes support structures hard to detach. Removal leaves scarring on the surface of the part. Bed Adhesion Issues : The material bonds too strongly to glass or PEI surfaces. Parts risk pulling up chunks of the build plate if a release agent is not used. Prone to Scratching : The high-gloss surface finish shows marks from handling and abrasive wear easily compared to the more matte-finish options of PLA. Slow Print Speeds : Achieving high quality requires reducing the movement speed of the extruder. Excessive speeds lead to poor bonding and surface defects. What are the Advantages of PLA Compared to PETG? The advantages of PLA compared to PETG are listed below. High Tensile Strength and Stiffness : The material offers excellent ultimate tensile strength for rigid applications. Parts remain stiff and do not deform easily under static loads. Flexibility and Toughness : Certain blends incorporate additives to improve impact resistance. Variations provide a balance between rigidity and resilience. Heat-treated (annealed) : PLA variants can withstand temperatures exceeding 80°C, surpassing standard PETG. Annealing processes reorganize the molecular structure to improve thermal limits. Chemical and Water Resistance : Standard PLA resists many organic solvents and oils. It maintains its shape in dry indoor environments for years. Good Layer Adhesion and Minimal Warping : Low thermal expansion ensures parts stay flat on the build plate. The material bonds well at relatively low temperatures. Versatile Printing Options : Printers without heated beds or enclosures handle the material successfully. A wide range of colors and aesthetic blends is readily available. Safe for Food and Medical Applications : Raw PLA resin is often biocompatible; however, 3D-printed parts require post-processing to meet safety standards for food contact or medical use. Longer-Term Durability : Parts kept in controlled indoor environments show minimal degradation over time. The material stays structurally sound if protected from high heat. Good for Mechanical Parts : High dimensional accuracy allows for tight tolerances in gear systems. Rigid walls provide the necessary support for internal mechanisms. Compatibility with PLA Prints : Multi-material systems use different PLA types to create complex geometries. Soluble supports bond effectively to the base material of Polylactic Acid during the process. What are the Disadvantages of PLA Compared to PETG? The disadvantages of PLA compared to PETG are listed below. Low Heat Resistance : Softening occurs at temperatures around 50°C. Parts left in a hot car warp or melt. Brittleness : Impact or sudden stress causes the material to shatter easily. It is unsuitable for parts experiencing heavy vibration or shocks. Biodegradability Concerns: Exposure to high moisture and microbes leads to material breakdown over long periods. It is not a permanent solution for outdoor use. Difficult Post-Processing : The low glass transition temperature causes the material to soften and gum up abrasives during high-speed sanding or polishing. Achieving a high-gloss finish requires specialized chemicals or techniques. Nozzle Clogging : Heat creep in the extruder causes the filament to swell and block the path. The issue is common during long prints in warm environments. Download Our FREE FDM Design Guide Download Now What are the Similarities Between PETG and PLA? The similarities between PETG and PLA are listed below. Thermoplastic Nature : PETG and PLA are both classified as thermoplastics, meaning they soften when heated and solidify upon cooling. This property allows for thermal processing, though repeated recycling cycles can lead to polymer chain scissoring. 3D Printing Compatibility : PETG and PLA are widely used in additive manufacturing due to their ease of extrusion and reliable print quality. Their compatibility with standard printing equipment makes them accessible for a broad range of applications. Cost-Effectiveness : PETG and PLA are relatively inexpensive compared to many engineering-grade polymers. Their affordability contributes to their popularity in prototyping and production. Color and Transparency Options : PETG and PLA can be produced in multiple colors and transparent grades. The versatility supports aesthetic and functional requirements in printed parts. Environmental Considerations : PLA is derived from renewable resources and is industrially compostable, while PETG is a petroleum-based plastic that is technically recyclable, making PLA and PETG 3D printing service suitable for sustainable manufacturing approaches when using closed-loop recycling. Desirable 3D printing attributes are rigidity, low cost, and speed of printing. PETG is a polyester, with glycol added to stabilize it and lower the melting temperature." TPU : This elastomeric thermoplastic provides high flexibility, elastic recovery, and vibration damping, with various grades offering flexibility comparable to commercial rubber materials. PLA is derived from renewable resources that offer higher biodegradability and lower thermal resistance. PETG is synthesized from petroleum-based compounds and provides greater durability and chemical resilience. Ductility differs between the two; PETG undergoes plastic deformation and bends under stress without fracturing, while PLA tends to snap when subjected to similar forces. Heat resistance favors PETG, which retains structural integrity at temperatures up to 70–75 °C, while PLA begins to deform near 50–55 °C. What are the Differences Between PETG and PLA? The differences between PETG and PLA are shown in the table below. PETG is functionally more flexible than PLA because of its higher ductility, which allows it to bend under stress whereas PLA remains rigid. PLA breaks or snaps when subjected to bending forces. PETG deforms and bends before reaching a point of failure. The material properties make PETG suitable for components requiring minor elastic deformation. The elongation at break for PETG remains higher than standard PLA. Is PETG more flexible than PLA? Yes, PETG exhibits greater practical flexibility than PLA. This is due to its superior ductility, which allows it to maintain its integrity through bending and impact. PLA tends to be brittle and shatters under stress. PETG maintains its integrity through bending and impact. What is the Melting Point of PETG compared to PLA? The melting point of PETG ranges between 230°C and 250°C compared to PLA, which melts at around 180°C to 220°C. Higher temperatures remain necessary for PETG to transition into a flowable state. PLA requires lower energy input for extrusion due to its chemical composition. Proper cooling becomes critical for PLA to prevent sagging. Thermal properties dictate the hardware requirements for each material. Printers must achieve a consistent PETG melting temperature. Accurate control is vital for managing the PETG melting point. Choosing the right material depends on the operating temperature of the final application. Users compare PETG filament vs PLA for functional parts. Environmental conditions influence the choice between PLA vs. PETG filament. Is PETG stronger than PLA? No, PLA is not stronger than PETG. Parts printed in PLA resist stretching more effectively than parts printed in PETG. The PETG offers better impact strength and durability despite its lower tensile rating. PLA parts fail abruptly through cracking. PETG parts tend to bend or deform before breaking. What are the Advantages of PETG Compared to PLA? The advantages of PETG compared to PLA are listed below.
